Man City's Enzo Fernandez dilemma: How Enzo Maresca can fix glaring midfield imbalance ahead of Fulham clash

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Oliver Thomas | 20 Nov 2026 17:09.
  • Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca faces an urgent tactical puzzle ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Fulham, as glaring structural flaws in his revamped midfield continue to leave the Sky Blues dangerously exposed on the counter-attack.
  • After kicking off his tenure at the Etihad Stadium with seven consecutive Premier League victories, the Italian has since overseen a jarring slump, suffering three straight top-flight defeats, most recently losing 3-1 at Nottingham Forest prior to the international break.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 20 Nov 2026 17:09.

Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca faces an urgent tactical puzzle ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Fulham, as glaring structural flaws in his revamped midfield continue to leave the Sky Blues dangerously exposed on the counter-attack.

After kicking off his tenure at the Etihad Stadium with seven consecutive Premier League victories, the Italian has since overseen a jarring slump, suffering three straight top-flight defeats, most recently losing 3-1 at Nottingham Forest prior to the international break.

While City's off-pitch turbulence regarding their financial charges case has dominated headlines, their recent on-pitch struggles stem largely from a £300m+ summer engine-room overhaul that has yet to find its rhythm.

Specifically, Maresca is grappling with how to integrate his two marquee £100m-plus acquisitions – Enzo Fernandez and Elliot Anderson – without sacrificing defensive solidity.

According to recent reports, throughout the opening months of the 2026-27 campaign, Man City have looked remarkably fragile whenever possession turns over. Only Newcastle United (20) have allowed more shots from fast breaks in the Premier League this term than the Citizens (17), who were sliced open repeatedly at the City Ground.

In that defeat to Forest, Maresca's side conceded eight fast breaks – the highest single-game tally by any top-flight club this season – and shipped two goals directly from rapid transitions.

The core issue lies in the incompatible profiles of Maresca's preferred central trio. Deploying Anderson alongside Fernandez in a double pivot behind playmaker Rayan Cherki creates a vacuum when City lose the ball.

Cherki contributes very little defensively, which places an unsustainable burden on the two deeper midfielders to screen the backline.

Rather than operating as a cohesive unit, Fernandez and Anderson frequently occupy the same right-sided zones, leaving the central and left-sided areas of the pitch wide open.

Premier League per-90 metrics (2025-26 vs. 2026-27).

Furthermore, Fernandez's defensive output has dipped noticeably since his £125m move from Chelsea; his tackle and possession-win rates per 90 minutes are down, while he struggled to impose himself physically against Forest.

While Forest duo Xaver Schlager and Ryan Yates dominated the battleground with 14 and 11 defensive contributions respectively, Fernandez managed just four – one fewer than Cherki (five).

Speaking at his pre-match press conference on Friday afternoon, Maresca was quick to shield his Argentine international from individual blame while acknowledging that tactical tweaks are required to restore equilibrium across the pitch.

"We won games with Enzo on the pitch," Maresca told reporters. "I know when there is a defeat we are all looking forward for the reason why and sometimes we think it's this or that.

"Sometimes probably we need more balance, different players on the pitch. It depends on the game. But we won games with Enzo, we lost games with Enzo. It's not just Enzo.

"But we are going to find solutions for more balance on the defensive line, in midfield and up front. I can't control what we pay for the players. People can think he's not going to make any mistake ever. He's a human being and he is going to make some mistakes.".

Recent findings suggest that with Pep Guardiola's former side having lost key control-oriented figures like Bernardo Silva and Rodri over the summer, Maresca cannot simply replicate his predecessor's blueprint. However, he does have the personnel to inject much-needed steel into his spine.

The most straightforward adjustment involves handing a bigger role to teenage summer arrival Ayyoub Bouaddi, who is widely regarded as one of the brightest young prospects in world football.

Restricted to just 177 Premier League minutes so far (two starts, three substitute outings) while adapting to English football, the athletic youngster offers the natural positional discipline and ball-winning instincts of a true holding number six.

Pairing the Moroccan ace with Anderson at the base of City’s midfield would help relieve the defensive strain on the England international and plug the gaps that several Premier League teams have ruthlessly exploited.

According to recent reports, crucially, introducing Bouaddi does not require banishing Fernandez to the substitutes' bench. Having pushed hard to bring the 25-year-old to Manchester just over two months ago, Maresca could instead move Fernandez further forward to operate at the apex of a midfield triangle in place of Cherki.

Fernandez’s ability to hold up play, draw fouls, time late runs into the penalty area and thread incisive passes makes him well-suited to an advanced role – provided he has two disciplined ball-winners anchoring the space behind him.

Man City enter Saturday's fixture boasting an extraordinary 20-match winning streak against Fulham in all competitions, having scored at least twice in every single one of those victories, yet memories of last season's chaotic 5-4 escape at Craven Cottage serve as a timely warning.

If Maresca fails to tighten his midfield structure this weekend, Man City's concerning vulnerability on the break threatens to derail their season before winter truly sets in.

Lamine Yamal mercilessly taunted England rival Elliot Anderson as tensions flared during the Three Lions’ spectacular victory over Spain on Sunday night.

England held on for a memorable 3-2 victory in Madrid after Anderson was given his marching orders with just under 30 minutes remaining.

Thomas Tuchel’s side were three goals in front and cruising when Anderson - looking to atone for a sloppy error from Jarrel Quansah - cynically hauled down 19-year-old Yamal as he barrelled down on goal.

Spain were awarded a penalty for the infringement, and Anderson was sent off - much to the Manchester City star’s bemusement.

But Yamal, aggrieved by Anderson’s challenge, made a beeline for the midfielder following the challenge. According to Spanish reports, the attacker mouthed ‘tonto, tonto’ to his rival following his dismissal.

The colloquial term can mean a number of things, varying from idiot, fool or stupid, but in any case is far from a term of affection.

🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨🚨بطاقة حمراء لإليوت أندرسون ولامين يامال يستفزه🤯🤯#اسبانيا_انجلترا #دوري_الأمم_الأوروبية pic.twitter.com/cOrswp5kCC.

Lamine Yamal was spotted taunting Elliot Anderson after the Manchester City midfielder was sent off for a challenge on the winger.

The moment came in England's historic 3-2 win over the World Champions.

Anderson blanked the 19-year-old while a VAR review confirmed the on-field official’s decision was the right one, eventually trudging off the pitch.

A fired-up Yamal galvanised the reigning world champions as they searched for an unlikely comeback.

Mikel Oyarzabal, the man who scored Spain’s winner against England two years ago in the 2024 Euros final, converted the spot kick before Nico Williams scored Spain’s second after latching on to an excellent Yamal cross.

However, Las Rojas fell short, with Sunday’s defeat their first in an imperious 43-game run.

A jubilant Thomas Tuchel hailed the match as his ‘best performance of my time as manager’.

Recent findings suggest that ‘What a performance we put out there for 60 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up,’ Tuchel noted after the game. ’Thirty minutes against Spain with ten men feels like three hours.

In a recent development, ‘It was a statement victory. It was on the highest level football-wise. It is a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.’.

Gameweek 11 of the 2026-27 Premier League season marks the return of one of Tottenham Hotspur's favourite sons, who now dons the red of Manchester United rather than lilywhite of Spurs.

Mauricio Pochettino's England homecoming is a daunting one, as Man United face old rivals Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday afternoon, needing at least a point to escape the bottom three of the Premier League table.

A stacked undercard precedes the Merseyside meeting, as the Red Devils' bitter rivals Manchester City kick off the gameweek at home to Fulham on Saturday lunchtime, bidding to avoid a fourth consecutive top-flight defeat.

Five 3pm kickoffs follow, as Coventry City tackle Thomas Frank's Crystal Palace, Tottenham Hotspur host Ipswich Town, Chelsea do battle with Leeds United, Aston Villa host Sunderland at Villa Park, and Bournemouth welcome Nottingham Forest to the South Coast.

Saturday concludes with champions Arsenal at one of their least favourite haunts - St James' Park - to take on Newcastle United, before Hull City and Brighton & Hove Albion occupy the 2pm Sunday slot.

Following the latest chapter in the Liverpool vs. Man Utd rivalry, gameweek 11 concludes with Brentford battling Everton at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Kasper Hogh and the missed Celtic Christmas advert trick as Martin O’Neill weighs up penalty dilemma

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Celtic Christmas advert was released on Friday containing the usual good cheer and a little festive pop at Rangers.
  • Sources indicate that all I want for Christmas is my first Parkhead goal.
  • Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Celtic Christmas advert was released on Friday containing the usual good cheer and a little festive pop at Rangers. It did, though, miss an obvious storyboard opportunity.

Sources indicate that all I want for Christmas is my first Parkhead goal. A sad-looking, shaggy-haired striker is seen traipsing through the snowy streets of the east end of Glasgow before bumping into a dreadlocked king of kings, who gives him the gift of putting the ball in the net.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Although Henrik Larrson is not involved, Kasper Hogh does in fact feature in the latest two-minute festive promo film, which has been released in conjunction with the Celtic FC Foundation’s Christmas appeal.

Industry observers note that callum McGregor calls out “Oi, youse two!” in the direction of Hogh and Benjamin Nygren. Viljami Sinisalo is more direct: “Kasper!” Nygren turns round, and indicates: “Who?”.

It has been revealed that it maybe doesn’t work as well when written down. Hogh – pronounced who - is clearly a good sport. However, as Martin O’Neill has stated on a number of occasions, and repeated on Friday at Lennoxtown, at some point strikers need to start scoring goals.

In a recent development, of course, Hogh thought he had finally bagged his first home goal in the hoops two weekends ago. Nygren set him up with a neat pass into the Dane’s path and seconds later the net billowed. Hogh celebrated with understandable gusto before the dismaying news that it was being ruled out for an innocuous foul in the build-up. “For him, that was a killer,” admitted O’Neill on the eve of the latest home game against St Mirren.

Recent findings suggest that all eyes will be on the team sheet. Will Hogh - yet to score after eight Parkhead appearances - play? Having been dropped from the Danish squad for their most recent games against Portugal and Norway, the striker was given some time off in the recent international window.

“He has been here, we have given him some time….he has had no break at all because where he came from (Norway) they were playing matches throughout (the summer),” explained O’Neill.

The manager made an extraordinary – to use one his favourite words - admission following the recent game against Kilmarnock, when Nygren wasted a spot kick. He claimed he would not have let Hogh take the penalty, which visiting keeper Nico Mantl saved, if the Dane had been on the park at the time.

Despite the ever more urgent need for Hogh to break his duck at home, O’Neill clearly felt the potential mental harm from failing to convert from 12 yards would have been too great a risk. The game, with Celtic winning 1-0 at the time, was also on a knife edge. A pressure penalty might not have been what Hogh needed.

Industry observers note that it will be interesting to see what happens against St Mirren if Celtic are awarded another penalty and Hogh is available to take it. One might expect the Dane to demand to be given the ball and put this ridiculous glitch to bed. Adding to the intrigue is that Nygren, who has an Achilles knock picked up on international duty with Sweden, might not play. Not that O’Neill trusts him from the spot now in any case.

The manager was not a fan of Nygren’s penalty technique against Kilmarnock. “All I will say is that if Nygren plays, which he may or may not, he won’t take it!” he stated. “All this (stuttered) walking up….why not just do an Alan Shearer and blast it into the net!? If you hit the goalkeeper, you’ll take his head off!”.

Sources indicate that non-scoring strikers is a theme just now given Oli McBurnie’s continued struggles at international level for Scotland. After just being subbed on, one wondered whether Sebastien Pocognoli might have ordered him to take the penalty against North Macedonia at Hampden Park last week. Again, with the manager’s future prospects possibly resting on the kick, maybe not. John McGinn did the necessary and Pocognoli survives, for the time being.

Hogh won’t want any handouts. He’s a centre forward who thrives on goals. He will feel capable of working it out for himself. No charity, please.

Industry observers note that as shown against Kilmarnock, he’s not far away. He missed one very good chance shortly after his chalked-off goal when one-on-one with Mantl. “If he had the first goal he would have taken that on another yard,” insisted O’Neill. “But that looked like a man in a real hurry to try and get his first (Celtic Park) goal.”.

In a recent development, easy going and charming, there are still limits to what Hogh can endure. He wouldn’t be human if it wasn’t having an effect.

In a recent development, “He seems philosophical about it at this minute,” O’Neill reported. “He thinks if he is working really hard for the side then he can get in….he should have taken a tip or two from Duran!”.

It has been revealed that camilo Duran is the opposite. With 13 goals in 21 appearances, he has made a flying start to his Celtic career.

Or maybe the aforementioned Larsson can make a visit. Like Hogh, the Swede was not an immediate hit at Parkhead.

O’Neill himself suggested Larsson could have some input - “The best thing for me to do is bring Henrik Larsson over and show him how to hit the ball into the net!” - when the discussion turned to players who initially laboured under great expectations.

Perhaps the late Trevor Francis, his old teammate, was one too? O’Neill was at Nottingham Forest when the striker arrived at the City Ground to become Britain’s first £1 million player. Talk about pressure.

“He took a couple of weeks,” remembered O’Neill. “It didn’t help that he had just been signed for a million pounds and Brian Clough told him to make the tea for everyone, which he did!

“First match, he made the tea for us in the dressing room! That wasn’t exactly what Trevor was expecting.” Hogh, who cost eleven times what Clough paid for Francis, has not been made to suffer such indignities - yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Bantams struggled for goals under latest manager Michael Duff until 11 in two cup matches last month, Swan scoring in both.

But with last week's game against Leicester City called off because of international call-ups, it has been a long wait to transfer that to League One.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The chance finally comes with Saturday's visit from Doncaster Rovers, promptly followed by another from Barnsley on Tuesday.

And Swan is convinced the way his side is playing, they will soon end a run which stands at three league games without a goal.

In a recent development, "When we're not scoring goals, the strikers in the team can feel like it's your fault," he admitted. "We're drawing 0-0 instead of winning 1-0, 2-0. But we're creating a lot of chances.

Sources indicate that "It's frustrating but we know they're going to start dropping. Once they do, we'll be just fine.

"The forward lads are starting to feel more confident. We just need that to translate to the league games now.

"I don't think it matters who you're playing against, finding the back of the net is massive for your confidence.".

Bradford's last league game was October's 3-0 defeat at home to Huddersfield Town.

"When you have two really strong (cup) performances you want to just keep going and take that momentum into the league," noted Swan.

"Now it's a chance to get a load of points and win a load of football games.

"It's going to be a tough period. We're going to need the whole team, with how many games there are. You can play Saturday, Tuesday, Saturday and all of a sudden you're nine points ahead of where you were before.

"Over Christmas and Upcoming Year, there's going to be a lot of games so there are a lot of chances to push higher up in the table.

"We were in a bit of a good rhythm going into the international break but we've had a good full week of training and we'll use Saturday to hopefully score a few goals and pick that momentum up again.".

Bobby Pointon's knee injury puts more emphasis on the other forwards, but Swan says it will inspire them.

Industry observers note that "Everyone in the front line will think we've got big shoes to fill there, because he's a class player," he argued. "We'll all do our best to step in and fill that role.".

The boyish, Lego-obsessed son of a farmer who quit Man City to become England's No 1: How James Trafford - with £95m spent on him - is maturing to star for Leeds and the Three Lions

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 14:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 16:35 EST, 16 November 2026.
  • 'It was like meeting a kid at a sixth-form careers day'.
  • When, at England's World Cup base in Kansas City, I then sat down with Trafford and he revealed that his partner had packed some Lego for him to build in camp, you wondered if sixth-form was a grade too high.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 14:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 16:35 EST, 16 November 2026.

'It was like meeting a kid at a sixth-form careers day'. That was the verdict, slightly unflattering but endearing all the same, of one Premier League chief after encountering James Trafford.

When, at England's World Cup base in Kansas City, I then sat down with Trafford and he revealed that his partner had packed some Lego for him to build in camp, you wondered if sixth-form was a grade too high.

It has been revealed that he is the son of a Cumbrian farmer and the Lego was of a tractor, which he would save for later in the tournament. 'You don't want to go too early,' he remarked.

Sources indicate that none of this is a criticism. Far from it. There was a boyish charm, an innocence, even, and Trafford was engaging tech giant. Nonetheless, he did not sound ready for the likes of a World Cup semi-final against Argentina. Thomas Tuchel agreed.

Industry observers note that but every boy will one day become a man. On a ferocious and febrile night in Madrid, no place for adolescents, we may just have witnessed James Trafford's graduation ceremony.

According to recent reports, without his double save in stoppage-time, England would have left Spain without a famous, and deserved, victory. One Spanish title labelled it 'la actuacion de su vida', the performance of his life. You wonder how much they saw of his loan spell at Accrington Stanley, but the sentiment stands.

James Trafford celebrates with Jarell Quansah, Dan Burn and Ezri Konsa during his starring performance in Spain.

Trafford pictured with his farmer father, David, in the cab of his tractor with their dogs (Source: James Trafford).

Sources indicate that madrid daily AS exclaimed: 'Magisterio de Trafford!' Translated, 'A Trafford Masterclass!'. They claim he was the reason Spain could not complete their comeback, and they would be right.

Sources indicate that when Tuchel stood with us in a corridor of the Metropolitano Stadium on the eve of the game, he had no problem confirming that Trafford would start. His message, though, was clear - it was sink or swim for a goalkeeper who turned 24 last month.

It has been revealed that not only did Trafford keep his head above water, it was he who pulled the team ashore. It was he to whom his senior colleagues ran in celebration. Ezri Konsa nearly took the shirt off Trafford's back, such was the force of his gratitude. But maybe this was the occasion when Trafford took the No 1 jersey from the back of Jordan Pickford, the holder for nearly a decade.

Pickford has done nothing wrong. Were Trafford to still display that maturity deficit, Pickford would be a reliable custodian heading to Euro 2028. This is not Peter Shilton post Italia 90, an uncomfortable truth of a great in need of the retirement barn. The 32-year-old has plenty to give on the back of all he has already given.

This, admitted Tuchel after the 3-2 win, is a selection dilemma that allows a manager to sleep well at night.

In a recent development, 'There is no headache at all!' he boomed. 'I'm so far away from a headache, I cannot imagine.

Trafford left Manchester City with the strategy to usurp Jordan Pickford as England No 1.

Jude Bellingham certainly seemed impressed with the performance of the goalkeeper.

'This is what we wanted. This is the best thing that can happen to all of us, also to Pickers. It is amazing how they push each other, and if then Traff has a performance like this, he has it because he knows he's well prepared. He gets the push from his colleagues and competitors.'.

Sources indicate that tuchel has seen enough of Trafford in training and around camp to believe he is ready for promotion. He has watched him for Leeds, where he rates as the best performing goalkeeper in the Premier League. His 'net goals prevented' (4.4) and 'save percentage' (81.4) are higher than any rival this season, including Pickford.

According to recent reports, 'You always have to deserve your place,' added Tuchel. 'You will never get a gift and just get a game (for the sake of it). So he deserved to play and we expected this kind of performance. It was not only the last save, but also the build-up play and not losing focus. He has proved it on this stage, so this gives him a lot of belief. Now, it's on him to keep going for it.'.

It, you presume, is the No 1 jersey. Trafford has made no secret of his desire to take it from Pickford, and he told us in the summer that such ambition was the motivation behind him wanting to leave Manchester City for a second time.

That day, he flipped his room key with a magician's sleight of hand throughout the interview, a dexterity useful for Lego. Better still for fingertip saves such as the one to deny Aymeric Laporte in the 91st minute.

Industry observers note that also in the gift pack from his girlfriend were two face masks. 'Very thoughtful,' he quipped. But that is another observation, bordering on concern, that some prospective buyers have made in recent years - on the goalkeeping scale of uber professional to joker, he resides too close to the latter. We have seen, even this season, the odd concentration lapse that speaks to that thought.

Trafford has played a starring role in goal since moving to Leeds United in the summer.

Industry observers note that but there was also a feeling that Trafford needed more exposure and responsibility before the penny dropped and his value was realised. Already, £95million has been spent on him in transfer fees.

At Leeds, and now with England, he has been given that stage, as Tuchel calls it. The head coach maintains that Pickford is his first choice, but it was Trafford he picked for both Nations League fixtures against Spain, the ones that really mattered, the ones that would strengthen or threaten his own employment.

As for Trafford's career prospects, to revisit our opening line, England's No 1 sounds like a fair vocation.

Thomas Tuchel wants England to use victory in the Nations League finals as a springboard to winning Euro 2028 at Wembley.

The head coach admits it has taken him a while to recover from the trauma of his side’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in July, for which he was heavily criticised.

But after beating world champions Spain 3-2 on Sunday night, topping their Nations League group ahead of March’s quarter-finals and next summer's finals, Tuchel is finally able to look forward with positivity and belief.

It has been revealed that ‘I saw the celebrations in Portugal when they won the Nations League,’ he stated. ‘It’s just the best, the best preparation we can have for the Euros. We want to have these matches on the highest level to prove ourselves and to gain confidence, to see where we are and to adjust our game where we need to, that’s what this Nations League is perfect for. We want to win it.’.

England have won five of their six matches since the World Cup, losing only to Spain at Wembley in September. In the build up to that game, Tuchel was involved in heated exchanges with observers who continued to question his tactics in the final half hour against Argentina.

’It took me a while to digest (the World Cup exit) and see the way forward, how we can help and adjust and improve, and how we can do this together,’ he said.

Industry observers note that ‘We had reviews and so on, but clarity then came together with the players. Straight away we had the energy right to take the next steps. The ideas became more clear for me, even if it was not so easy the first week, to overcome and arrive with different emotions. Some were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not digested it. But it was important to have this kind of process together.

‘(Spain) was a complete performance that makes me very proud. It's a full package of belief, of courage, of commitment, of togetherness, of relying on each other and stepping up in this moment.’.

Tuchel, though, has rejected the idea that seeing out the win Madrid was proof that he has learned from his mistakes in Atlanta.

‘Not at all, I think we would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11,’ he said. ‘For me, it was Mexico reloaded (not Argentina). It's one man down, but what can you do? It is their strength to have ball possession, to overload and find the gaps. It just plays totally into their hands and it comes wave after wave. It felt like three hours and thirty minutes!’.

Duncan Ferguson was sent off as his unbeaten start as Glentoran manager came grinding to a halt in a 3-2 defeat at Cliftonville in the NIFL Premiership on Friday night.

The former Rangers and Everton striker was shown a straight red card and ordered from the touchline after losing his temper in the aftermath of his side falling behind at Solitude in north Belfast.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Ferguson had angrily protested against Cliftonville's opener believing there was a foul on defender Jarlath O'Rourke in the build-up and was subsequently sent to the stand by referee Ben McMaster.

Ironically, Glentoran had already equalised by the time the card was brandished with Cal Weatherup levelling the match at 1-1 just a minute after Joseph Sheridan had put the hosts in front.

The red card was Ferguson's first as a manager in his 80th appearance in the dugout but the 10th of his career overall after receiving his marching orders on nine occasions during his playing days.

Assistant manager Gary Bollan took charge for the remainder of the game as Glentoran fell behind to a Brian Healy strike in the 67th minute before equalising again through James Douglas with four minutes left.

However, Cliftonville took the three points thanks to a second goal of the night from Sheridan in the 88th minute.

Bollan handled post-match media duties as Ferguson kept his counsel.

Industry observers note that "I think the manager got frustrated because it was a foul," Bollan mentioned. "It changes the dynamic [the sending off], he's a leader. I've then got to step in and fill his boots and it's a massive set of boots to fill.".

In the NIFL Premiership, a manager or team official given a red card receives an automatic one-match suspension for the next competitive fixture, with longer bans possible depending on the offence.

It means the former Scotland international will not be in the dugout for the Northern Ireland League Cup match against Larne at The BetMcLean Oval on Tuesday with any further punishment dependent on the content of the referee’s report.

Ferguson had started his Glentoran tenure with two away draws against Coleraine and Carrick before winning his first home game in charge 2-1 against Bangor last Friday. The defeat leaves Glentoran 14 points behind league leaders Linfield.

Tech Report: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 91 min read (18165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~91 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics1,2.
  • Recent findings suggest that cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and is often considered to be an adaptive behaviour driven by ecological or social pressures1,2.
  • In a recent development, locusts provide a compelling model for studies of cannibalism because of its vital role in collective dynamics5,6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics1,2. Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented2, the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria, guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei. Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

Recent findings suggest that cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and is often considered to be an adaptive behaviour driven by ecological or social pressures1,2. However, its occurrence is highly context-dependent, and the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. In humans, cannibalism largely disappeared with cultural evolution, partly owing to prion diseases3. Similarly, insects such as crickets rarely engage in cannibalism under normal conditions, but confinement or nutritional deprivation can trigger this behaviour4. These observations highlight the influence of environmental pressures on cannibalism, although its intrinsic regulatory mechanisms remain unclear.

In a recent development, locusts provide a compelling model for studies of cannibalism because of its vital role in collective dynamics5,6. In juvenile migratory bands, the threat of conspecific predation from behind promotes forward movement, reducing cannibalistic risk and contributing to group cohesion5,6. Cannibalism also provides nutritional benefits, allowing locusts to compensate for food deficiencies and potentially enhancing survival and movement capacity7,8. This behaviour is strongly influenced by density-dependent phase polyphenism. At low densities, solitarious locusts avoid conspecifics, whereas increased population density promotes gregarious behaviour and cannibalistic encounters5,7. Nutritional deficiencies further exacerbate cannibalism. Field studies of South American locusts (Schistocerca cancellata) have demonstrated that carbohydrate deprivation promotes cannibalism9, whereas laboratory studies on desert locusts (Schistocerca gregaria) have shown that protein-biased diets reduce movement and increase cannibalistic interactions7. Although these findings establish the ecological importance of cannibalism, its molecular and genetic regulation remains poorly understood.

Chemical cues regulate diverse locust behaviours, including aggregation10,11, oviposition12, mating13 and cannibalism14. Our previous work identified phenylacetonitrile (PAN) as a density-dependent anticannibalistic pheromone that activates specific olfactory receptors and reduces conspecific predation in crowded populations14. However, whether chemical cues actively induce cannibalism has remained unclear. Field and laboratory observations indicate that injured locusts are preferentially targeted by conspecifics15, suggesting that injury-induced chemical signals may attract individuals and promote cannibalistic behaviour.

Sources indicate that guaiacol, a volatile compound produced by gut microbiota during plant digestion, has been identified as an aggregation pheromone in desert locusts16. Here we show that injury-induced microbiota-derived guaiacol coordinates immune defence and cannibalism in migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria) and elucidate the underlying mechanisms, which span microbial biosynthesis, olfactory detection, immune regulation and behavioural responses. Together, our findings identify a microbial signalling mechanism linking immunity and cannibalism, revealing how host–microbe interactions mediate a trade-off between immune protection and vulnerability to conspecific predation.

Industry observers note that cannibalism in L. migratoria exhibits phase polyphenism, with solitarious nymphs typically avoiding conspecific predation, whereas gregarious nymphs are more prone to engage in cannibalism, particularly under conditions of crowding or food scarcity14. Preliminary observations indicated that injured individuals were rapidly surrounded and attacked by nearby conspecifics (Fig. 1a), suggesting that injury itself serves as a cue that increases susceptibility to conspecific predation. To test this hypothesis, we conducted dual-choice assays with gregarious fourth- and fifth-instar nymphs, the developmental stages at which cannibalism is most prevalent14. As injury can alter locomotor performance and therefore influence predator choice independently of injury-derived signals, we controlled for this potentially confounding factor by immobilizing both prey individuals. This experimental design enabled us to specifically evaluate the contribution of injury-associated cues to predator preference. In each assay, pairs of immobilized intact and injured fourth-instar nymphs were presented at opposite ends of a chamber containing ten starved fifth-instar predators (Fig. 1b). Injuries were induced either mechanically or by previous conspecific bites. Across all assays, predators consistently exhibited a marked predation preference for injured over intact prey, indicating a significant role of injury in heightening vulnerability to conspecific predation (Fig. 1c).

a, Representative image of fifth-instar gregarious nymphs attacking an injured fourth-instar gregarious nymph. b, Schematic of the dual-choice predation assay. Ten starved fifth-instar gregarious nymphs were presented with one intact and one injured fourth-instar nymph immobilized at opposite ends of the arena. c–f, Predation preferences of intact (c; n = 15; group 1, P = 0.009; group 2, P = 0.012), ommatidectomized (d; n = 15; group 1, P = 0.001; group 2, P = 0.006), antennectomized (e; n = 15) and LmOrco−/− (f; n = 14) nymphs. Three prey pairings were tested: group 1, intact versus bitten; group 2, intact versus mechanically injured; group 3, mechanically injured versus bitten. g, Schematic of the dual-choice olfactometer assay testing volatiles from intact and injured fourth-instar nymphs. h,i, Olfactory preference of wild-type (h; n = 19; group 1, P = 0.010; group 2, P < 0.001) and LmOrco−/− (i; n = 15) nymphs for the three pairings described above. In c–f, preference is expressed as the percentage of total prey body mass consumed from each prey individual. All behavioural data are presented as box-and-whisker plots (boxes represent median and upper/lower quartiles; centre lines indicate the median, plus signs indicate the mean and whiskers extend from the minimum to the maximum values). Statistical analyses were performed using two-sided paired-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. ***P < 0.001; ** P < 0.01; * P < 0.05; NS, not significant.

To determine whether the type of injury influenced predation preference, we compared predator preferences between mechanically injured and bitten prey. No significant difference was observed (Fig. 1c), indicating that injury alone, regardless of its origin, is sufficient to induce preferential predation. To explore whether injury-induced vulnerability was consistent across developmental stages, we extended the assays to first- to fifth-instar nymphs as prey. In all stages tested, fifth-instar predators consistently preferred injured prey over their intact counterparts, irrespective of injury type (Extended Data Fig. 1a). These findings demonstrate that injury-driven cannibalism is a robust and consistent trait across the development of gregarious locusts.

According to recent reports, next, we investigated the sensory cues mediating injury-induced predation. To assess the roles of olfactory and visual inputs, we performed antennal ablation (disrupting primary olfactory input), knocked out olfactory coreceptor LmOrco (disrupting olfactory receptor function) (Extended Data Fig. 1b) or removed the compound eyes (disrupting visual input). Predators with removed compound eyes retained their preference for injured prey (Fig. 1d), suggesting that visual cues are not required to mediate this behaviour. By contrast, predators lacking antennae or LmOrco function revealed no preference for injured over intact prey (Fig. 1e,f). Notably, although antennectomized predators no longer exhibited a statistically significant preference, a weak residual bias towards injured prey remained (Fig. 1e). This observation was consistent with the anatomical organization of the locust olfactory system, in which the antennae constitute the principal but not the exclusive olfactory organs. Consequently, antennal removal might substantially reduce but not completely eliminate olfactory perception. By contrast, disruption of LmOrco, which broadly impairs odorant receptor function, resulted in a complete loss of discriminatory behaviour (Fig. 1f). Together, these findings identify LmOrco-dependent olfaction as the primary sensory modality mediating injury-induced cannibalistic predation.

It has been revealed that finally, we assessed whether volatile chemical cues contributed to the observed predation bias. Headspace volatiles from both injured and intact nymphs were collected and presented in a dual-choice olfactometer (Fig. 1g). Starved fifth-instar predators strongly preferred the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals over the zone containing volatiles from intact prey (Fig. 1h). No significant difference in preference was observed between volatiles from mechanically versus bitten prey (Fig. 1h), indicating that injury-induced volatile release enhances predator attraction, thereby increasing the susceptibility of injured individuals to cannibalism. By contrast, LmOrco−/− predators indicated no preference for the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals (Fig. 1i), indicating that LmOrco-dependent olfaction mediated the predation preference.

It has been revealed that to investigate the chemical signals underlying injury-induced cannibalism in L. migratoria, we analysed the headspace volatiles emitted by intact, mechanically injured and bitten locust nymphs (Fig. 2a). Among the compounds detected, guaiacol emerged as the dominant injury-affected odorant (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Table 1), with emission levels approximately ten-fold higher in injured nymphs compared with intact controls and gregarious adults (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This increase in guaiacol release was consistent across all developmental instars (first to fifth) (Extended Data Fig. 2c), suggesting that an increase in guaiacol production is a consistent physiological response to injury in gregarious nymphs. By contrast, other compounds—including PAN, which has previously been linked to suppression of cannibalism14—showed no significant changes across injury conditions (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2d), indicating that guaiacol is a key injury cue.

It has been revealed that to assess the behavioural significance of guaiacol, we conducted dual-choice olfactometer assays with fifth-instar nymphs and male and female adults from both gregarious and solitarious phases, testing the effects of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Table 2) at a concentration of 10−3 (Fig. 2d). Only gregarious nymphs exhibited strong attraction to guaiacol; solitarious individuals and gregarious adults indicated no significant preference (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Video 1). This indicated that guaiacol selectively attracts gregarious nymphs. We then investigated whether the naturally emitted levels of guaiacol from injured gregarious nymphs were sufficient to trigger attraction. Quantitative headspace analysis showed that emissions from injured gregarious nymphs corresponded to concentrations equivalent to 10−5 to 10−4 dilutions of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2e). To determine whether these natural guaiacol emissions were sufficient to induce attraction, we tested behavioural responses of gregarious nymphs using a full concentration series (10−7 to 10−2) in a two-choice olfactometer (Fig. 2d). Attraction to guaiacol emerged sharply at 10−6 and remained robust at higher concentrations but disappeared at 10−7 (Fig. 2f). This aligned with the physiological range of natural emissions from injured nymphs, confirming that guaiacol concentrations released by injured individuals are behaviourally relevant. As all preceding behavioural assays were conducted with individually tested locusts, we next examined whether guaiacol attraction was preserved under the social conditions that characterize gregarious populations. To address this question, we performed dual-choice olfactometer assays using groups of five gregarious nymphs and quantified the average time spent by the group on each side of the arena. Consistent with the results obtained from individually tested animals, groups of gregarious nymphs spent significantly more time on the side containing 10−3 guaiacol than on the control side (Extended Data Fig. 2f and Supplementary Video 2). These findings demonstrate that the attractive effect of guaiacol persists in a group context and therefore probably operates under ecologically relevant social conditions.

In a recent development, as attraction alone does not necessarily imply a decision to engage in cannibalistic behaviour, we next investigated whether guaiacol could directly trigger cannibalistic predation. We performed two-choice predation assays, providing pairs of intact fourth-instar gregarious nymphs—one treated with 2 µl of 10−4 guaiacol (representing natural emission levels from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) and the other with solvent oil—to 10 starved fifth-instar gregarious predators (Fig. 2g). Guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially consumed, whereas solvent-treated nymphs were rarely attacked (Fig. 2h), confirming that guaiacol is a potent elicitor of cannibalistic predation. We then sought to rule out the potential influence of endogenous guaiacol on predator preference. Previous studies have shown that guaiacol is primarily synthesized by gut microbiota during plant digestion in locusts16. To eliminate this confounding factor, we generated germ-depleted gregarious nymphs by administering a cocktail of three antibiotics (tetracycline, streptomycin and ciprofloxacin) in their feed17,18,19 (Fig. 2i). This approach effectively abolished guaiacol emission in both intact and injured nymphs, providing a chemically clean background for subsequent behavioural assays (Fig. 2j). We then treated the germ-depleted gregarious nymphs with 2 µl of either 10−4 guaiacol (mimicking natural release from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) or solvent oil and used them as prey in dual-choice predation assays (Fig. 2i). As observed previously, guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially attacked, and solvent-treated nymphs were largely ignored (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 2g). Finally, to evaluate the ecological relevance of guaiacol-mediated cannibalism under more naturalistic conditions, we performed semi-field experiments in large outdoor mesh enclosures (1.8 m × 1.2 m × 1.5 m). Each enclosure contained 500 fifth-instar gregarious predators, together with 100 fourth-instar prey perfumed with either 10−4 guaiacol or solvent alone (Extended Data Fig. 2h). After 24 h, substantially fewer fourth-instar nymphs remained in guaiacol-treated enclosures than in control enclosures, indicating a significantly higher frequency of cannibalistic interactions in the presence of guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Consistent with direct behavioural observations, the reduction in surviving individuals was attributable to increased conspecific predation rather than escape, as all locusts were confined within the enclosure. These findings demonstrate that guaiacol-mediated promotion of cannibalism persists at the population level under seminatural conditions, supporting the ecological relevance of this injury-associated signal. Collectively, these findings establish guaiacol as a critical chemical cue that both signals injury and induces conspecific predation.

To elucidate the molecular basis of guaiacol detection in L. migratoria, we sought to identify the specific olfactory receptors involved. In our previous study, we identified LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 as receptors responsive to guaiacol, on the basis of functional characterization of 49 L. migratoria olfactory receptors20. To confirm whether other olfactory receptors were involved in detection of this compound, we expanded our analysis to include a panel of 82 of approximately 140 identified L. migratoria olfactory receptors (Fig. 3a). Consistent with our earlier findings, LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 exhibited robust responses to guaiacol in a heterologous expression system (Fig. 3a,b), while no other receptor showed comparable sensitivity.

All receptor response data were generated in this study. c, Representative SSR traces from locust basiconic sensilla (S. basiconic) and trichoid sensilla (S. trichoid) in response to 10−1 guaiacol. Scanning electron micrographs of both sensillum types are shown14; yellow bar indicates stimulus duration. d, EAG dose–response curves for guaiacol in wild-type (WT; n = 15), LmOR34−/− (n = 20; 10−4 to 10−1, all P < 0.001), LmOR36−/− (n = 18; 10−1, P = 0.002; 10−2, P = 0.031) and LmOR39−/− (n = 15) nymphs. e, SSR dose–response curves in wild-type (n = 30), LmOR34−/− (n = 30; 10−3 to 10−1, all P < 0.001; 10−4, P = 0.001), LmOR36−/− (n = 30; 10−1, P < 0.001; 10−2, P = 0.005; 10−3, P = 0.040) and LmOR39−/− (n = 28) nymphs. f, Behavioural responses of mutant nymphs to 10−3 guaiacol (n = 20; LmOR39−/−, P = 0.024). g, Predation preferences of mutant nymphs between freely moving germ-depleted nymphs treated with 2 µl of 10−4 guaiacol or solvent (n = 16; LmOR39−/−, P < 0.001). Data are mean ± s.e.m. (d and e) or box-and-whisker plots (f and g; boxes, interquartile range; centre lines, medians; plus signs, means; whiskers, minima and maxima). Statistical significance was assessed using two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests (d and e) or two-sided paired-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (f and g). ***P < 0.001; **P < 0.01; *P < 0.05. It has been revealed that olfactory sensory neurons expressing different olfactory receptors are localized in distinct sensilla on the antennae of L. migratoria. To identify the sensilla responsible for guaiacol detection, we performed single-sensillum recordings (SSR) from basiconic and trichoid sensilla, which contain neurons expressing coreceptor Orco21,22. Basiconic sensilla harbour a larger population of sensory neurons (20–50), whereas trichoid sensilla contain only 2 or 3 neurons14. Owing to the higher neuronal density in basiconic sensilla, individual responses could not be distinguished on the basis of action potential amplitudes. Therefore, we measured the aggregate response of the entire neuronal population within the sensillum. Strong neuronal responses to guaiacol were detected in basiconic sensilla, whereas no response was observed in trichoid sensilla (Fig. 3c).

Sources indicate that inconsistent results were noted between electrophysiological and behavioural tests with respect to active concentrations of guaiacol, with a significantly higher threshold in the electrophysiological experiments. However, when we used solid-phase microextraction (SPME) technology to measure the concentration that actually reached the antenna during stimulation in the electrophysiological experiments, we found that the amount of guaiacol was comparable with the 10−6 dilution used in the behavioural assays (Extended Data Fig. 3a).

To assess the functional contribution of the LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 genes in vivo, we generated targeted loss-of-function mutants using CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome editing. Guide RNAs (Extended Data Table 3) targeting the first exon of these genes produced frame-shift deletions of 235 bp (LmOR34) (Extended Data Fig. 3b), 262 bp (LmOR36) (Extended Data Fig. 3b) and 8 bp (LmOR39) (Extended Data Fig. 3b), resulting in predicted truncations of the encoded proteins. Electroantennography (EAG) recordings indicated that the guaiacol-induced response was significantly reduced in LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants compared with wild-type nymphs, whereas the response in LmOR39−/− mutants remained unchanged (Fig. 3d). Furthermore, SSR recordings from basiconic sensilla demonstrated that neuronal response to guaiacol was significantly reduced in the LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants compared with wild-type nymphs, whereas LmOR39−/− locusts exhibited robust responses (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 3c). Taken together, these data indicate key roles of both LmOR34 and LmOR36 in mediation of the detection of guaiacol. We then investigated the behavioural consequences of these receptor disruptions. LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants showed a complete lack of attraction to guaiacol (Fig. 3f), in contrast to wild-type controls, which exhibited robust attraction. This loss of attraction was accompanied by a marked impairment in predation preference for guaiacol-treated prey nymphs (Fig. 3g). By contrast, the LmOR39−/− mutants showed no alteration in their behavioural and predation preferences (Fig. 3f,g), suggesting that LmOR34 and LmOR36 are essential for mediation of the behavioural response to guaiacol.

Our previous study indicated that LmOR34 and LmOR36 also responded strongly to 2,4,6-trimethylpyridine (2,4,6-TMP)20 (Extended Data Fig. 3d), a compound that is highly attractive to gregarious locusts. To test whether this compound also promoted cannibalistic behaviour, we performed dual-choice predation assays (Extended Data Fig. 3e), presenting prey nymphs treated with either 2,4,6-TMP or solvent to starved gregarious predators. Predator nymphs showed no significant preference for 2,4,6-TMP-treated prey compared with controls (Extended Data Fig. 3e). These results showed that although 2,4,6-TMP is a potent attractant, it does not directly promote cannibalism, confirming that this compound has other ecological functions. To directly compare the effects of guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP on cannibalistic behaviour, we conducted a second dual-choice assay, in which prey nymphs were treated with either guaiacol or 2,4,6-TMP, both at a 10−4 dilution. Predator nymphs showed a strong preference for guaiacol-treated prey over 2,4,6-TMP-treated prey (Extended Data Fig. 3e). To further examine whether the observed predatory preference reflected a general response to behaviourally attractive locust volatiles, we performed a further dual-choice predation assay using 4-vinylanisole (4VA), another attractive locust odorant10. Predators were simultaneously offered two germ-depleted gregarious nymphs, one treated with 2 μl of a 10−4 dilution of guaiacol and the other with an equal volume of a 10−4 dilution of 4VA. Predator nymphs showed a significantly stronger preference for attacking and biting guaiacol-treated prey than 4VA-treated prey (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Together, these results demonstrate that enhanced predatory responses are not elicited by attractive locust volatiles in general but are specific to guaiacol, identifying guaiacol as a specialized chemical cue that promotes cannibalistic behaviour.

It has been revealed that notably, ligand-specific behavioural divergence despite shared receptor components has been widely documented across insects, including model species Drosophila melanogaster23,24, in which differential peripheral tuning25 and downstream circuit integration enable discrimination of chemically related cues26. To examine whether similar mechanisms operated in locusts, we compared the response properties of LmOR34 and LmOR36 to guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP. Although both ligands activated both receptors, guaiacol elicited markedly stronger and more sensitive responses than 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3f,g). Moreover, the response kinetics of LmOR34 and LmOR36 differed substantially between guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), indicating that these ligands impose distinct temporal activation patterns at the receptor level that could be differentially decoded by downstream circuits. In addition to receptor-intrinsic differences, ligand-specific behaviours are likely to be shaped by distinct population-level coding in the antennal lobe. Consistent with this idea, our previous study showed that the antennal lobe activation patterns evoked by guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP only partially overlapped27, suggesting other receptor inputs. For example, LmOR46 responds to 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3d), whereas LmOR39 responds to guaiacol (Fig. 3b). Furthermore, because only 82 of the 140 predicted L. migratoria olfactory receptors have been functionally characterized, other receptors may remain unidentified. Although these receptors may contribute only modestly to odour detection, even weak inputs could reshape ensemble coding in the antennal lobe, thereby biasing downstream circuit activation towards distinct ecological and behavioural outcomes. Together, differential receptor tuning (sensitivity and kinetics) and ligand-specific recruitment of other receptors probably explain why guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP produce divergent behavioural consequences despite engaging shared receptors.

Industry observers note that guaiacol has previously been identified as a volatile produced by Pantoea agglomerans in the gut of S. gregaria and has been implicated in locust behaviour16. To identify guaiacol-producing bacteria in L. migratoria, we performed gut microbiota metagenomic sequencing but did not detect P. agglomerans (Fig. 4a), suggesting alternative microbial sources. We subsequently isolated cultivable bacteria from the gut and haemolymph of fourth-instar gregarious nymphs (Fig. 4b). Screening of more than 50 colonies identified a guaiacol-producing isolate from both tissues (Fig. 4b,c), which whole-genome sequencing identified as Enterobacter hormaechei, a dominant gut bacterium (Fig. 4a). Metagenomic analyses further confirmed high abundance of this bacterium in both the gut and haemolymph (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Although E. hormaechei was not reported in a previous study of the L. migratoria microbiome28, metagenomic sequencing and quantitative PCR (qPCR) detected it in all six geographically distinct field populations examined, with varying relative abundances (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Screening of other isolates also identified Klebsiella pneumoniae as a guaiacol producer, with emission levels comparable with those of E. hormaechei (Fig. 4c). However, we selected E. hormaechei for subsequent mechanistic analyses as it was consistently detected across samples and populations and exhibited stable guaiacol production.

Prey moved freely (l, m and r). Data are mean ± s.e.m. (d–f) or box plots (boxes, interquartile range; lines, medians; plus signs, means; whiskers, range). Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used, except in f (Pearson correlation). Independent individuals were used at each time point in d–f. Haemolymph (approximately 5 μl per locust) was pooled from 20 individuals per biological replicate. ***P < 0.001; **P < 0.01; *P < 0.05.

Industry observers note that we next examined the relationships of injury with bacterial abundance and guaiacol emission. Following injury, both haemolymph bacterial loads (Fig. 4d) and guaiacol emission (Fig. 4e) increased over time, peaking approximately 6 h after injury and stabilizing at around 8 h (Fig. 4d,e), and their temporal changes were positively correlated (Fig. 4f). To assess localized bacterial enrichment, we collected equal volumes of haemolymph from wound sites and intact regions of the same individuals 6 h after injury (Fig. 4g). Wound-site haemolymph had significantly higher bacterial loads (Fig. 4h) and guaiacol levels (Fig. 4i), indicating localized accumulation of E. hormaechei and enhanced guaiacol production. As population density can influence locust gut microbiota29, we also compared E. hormaechei abundance between phases and found no significant difference between solitarious and gregarious nymphs (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

It has been revealed that to determine whether E. hormaechei influenced locust behaviour, we first tested its volatiles in a two-choice olfactometer (Fig. 4j). Gregarious nymphs were significantly attracted to bacterial volatiles relative to the control medium (Fig. 4k). We then examined whether these volatiles promoted cannibalism using dual-choice predation assays (Fig. 4l). Two mechanically injured germ-depleted prey nymphs, matched for injury size and location, were presented simultaneously to ten starved fifth-instar gregarious predators, with one prey recolonized with E. hormaechei and the other left untreated. Predators preferentially attacked and consumed prey harbouring E. hormaechei, whereas germ-depleted controls were rarely targeted (Fig. 4m).

To identify the genetic basis of guaiacol biosynthesis, we sequenced the E. hormaechei genome and identified a cluster of three vanillic acid decarboxylase (vdc) genes, which have been previously implicated in microbial conversion of vanillic acid to guaiacol30 (Fig. 4n). Heterologous expression of this cluster in Escherichia coli (Extended Data Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 1) confirmed its capacity to catalyse guaiacol production from vanillic acid in vitro (Fig. 4o). Conversely, deletion of the vdc genes in E. hormaechei (Extended Data Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 1) completely abolished guaiacol production, as confirmed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) (Fig. 4p). These findings establish an essential role of this gene cluster in guaiacol biosynthesis.

Finally, we assessed whether microbial guaiacol biosynthesis was required for locust attraction and cannibalism. In two-choice olfactometer assays, gregarious nymphs were attracted to volatiles from wild-type E. hormaechei but not vdc-deficient mutants (Fig. 4q). Similarly, in dual-choice predation assays, starved gregarious predators preferentially attacked mechanically injured germ-depleted prey recolonized with wild-type E. hormaechei, whereas prey harbouring vdc mutants were rarely targeted despite identical injury size and location (Fig. 4r). Together, these results demonstrate that injury-associated guaiacol production by E. hormaechei is essential for converting host injury into an olfactory cue that promotes conspecific attraction and cannibalism.

Industry observers note that injured gregarious nymphs release elevated levels of guaiacol despite the increased risk of conspecific cannibalism. This raises the question of why such a seemingly costly response is maintained. We considered that guaiacol release might provide compensatory benefits to injured individuals. To explore this possibility, we first considered the antimicrobial properties of guaiacol. Previous studies have shown that guaiacol can inhibit or kill a broad range of microorganisms, including bacteria and fungi; these activities were attributed to its phenolic structure, which disrupts microbial membranes and interferes with metabolic processes31,32,33. On the basis of these properties, we proposed that guaiacol produced by E. hormaechei could provide immune benefits to injured gregarious nymphs by suppressing pathogen invasion.

Industry observers note that to test this hypothesis, we selected two pathogens commonly associated with locust mortality: intrinsic locust bacterial pathogen Proteus mirabilis34 (Extended Data Fig. 5a) and commercially available fungal insecticide Metarhizium anisopliae35 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). To determine whether guaiacol could improve resistance to pathogen invasion following injury, we used germ-depleted gregarious nymphs, which were either fed guaiacol or left untreated, and infected them with either wild-type E. hormaechei or its vdc knockout mutant (Fig. 5a). After manually injuring the nymphs, we applied infections with both M. anisopliae and P. mirabilis to the wound sites and monitored survival over several days (Fig. 5a). We found that guaiacol-fed or wild-type E. hormaechei-infected nymphs exhibited significantly higher survival rates compared with those that were non-fed or infected with the vdc-mutant E. hormaechei (Fig. 5b,c). These results indicated that guaiacol, produced by E. hormaechei, might enhance the survival of injured nymphs when exposed to pathogen infection. To confirm that this protective effect was due to the ability of guaiacol to inhibit pathogen proliferation, we quantified pathogen loads in the haemolymph of guaiacol-fed and non-fed nymphs, as well as in those infected with wild-type or vdc-mutant E. hormaechei. We observed that pathogen burdens were significantly higher in the haemolymph of non-fed and vdc-mutant-infected nymphs compared with guaiacol-fed and wild-type E. hormaechei-infected nymphs (Fig. 5d,e). These findings support the notion that guaiacol production by E. hormaechei suppresses invasion and proliferation of M. anisopliae and P. mirabilis, thereby providing immune benefits to injured locusts. Finally, to determine whether the protective effect of guaiacol-producing E. hormaechei was pathogen-specific or broadly applicable, we infected injured locusts with another opportunistic pathogen, Enterococcus faecalis34 (Extended Data Fig. 5c). As observed for P. mirabilis and M. anisopliae, guaiacol supplementation and colonization by wild-type E. hormaechei significantly suppressed pathogen infection (Extended Data Fig. 5d) and enhanced host survival (Extended Data Fig. 5e). Together, these results indicate that guaiacol functions as a broadly protective microbial metabolite that enhances host defence against diverse pathogens following injury.
