Enzo Maresca believes streetwise Enzo Fernández will give Manchester City an extra winning edge – as he told his record £125 million signing to forget about the size of the fee.

City made the Argentina midfielder the joint most expensive purchase in Premier League history with their deadline day swoop from Chelsea.

Maresca has opted against naming Fernández among his captains’ leadership group, which features Ruben Dias, Erling Haaland, Marc Guéhi and Gianluigi Donnarumma.

But the Italian – who knows Fernández well from their time together at Stamford Bridge – is confident his fierce competitive instincts will bring an added dimension to his side.

“I don’t know if it’s streetwise but he knows how to win,” Maresca said, who is in line to hand Fernández his debut against Coventry on Saturday. “When you want to compete or win, it’s much more important to have players that already know how to do that than players who have never done it in the past.

Recent findings suggest that “Enzo is not the only one. This squad has many players who know how to win titles and how to compete and this is what we are looking for.

Sources indicate that “I know Enzo quite well and I know what he can bring to the team. He is a winner, [has] a winner’s mentality and knows how to win [after] the World Cup, Club World Cup [success].

“I just noted he is a winner and when you belong to the squad and another winning player arrives, they are always happy.

“I can promise you that in the last four or five days, four or five players from the squad were asking if was coming or not because they wanted him to be with us. It’s very vital that he is with us.”.

In a recent development, maresca said he planned to use Fernandez predominantly as a No 6 or No 8 depending on the game. “I see Enzo as a six, a little bit more deep, or [an eight] a little higher arriving in the box,” he said.

Sources indicate that good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Saturday afternoon 3pm kick-offs of which we are treated to a rare number this week as Sky and TNT Sports decide to inconvenience only 10 sets of matchgoing supporters rather than the usual 12 or 14. The matches start, purely alphabetically, with unbeaten Brentford hosting Sunderland, Leeds United travelling to Brighton and Hove Albion’s Amex Stadium where they have never won and have come away with only three points in their seven visits, the something’s-got-to-give quasi derby between winless Fulham and pointless Palace, leaders Man City hosting Coventry City for the Sky Blue Cup and Tottenham head to Nottingham Forest in pursuit of their first point to spoil the gaiety of a nation.

In a recent development, we have Mike McGrath reporting from the Etihad and John Percy at the City Ground and I will endeavour to keep you up to date with developments at the other three grounds via various methods. Forest vs Spurs seems the most consequential of the fixtures, not because either manager is in any danger but because now the window has closed it should give us a clearer picture of how Roberto De Zerbi intends to marshal his surfeit of wingers into a coherent attack that can break their goalscoring duck and how he proposes to organise a back four that have shipped five goals.

Fulham and Palace have come in for a lot of criticism regarding their recruitment and while I can understand the frustration of the former’s fans for doing so much business with Real Madrid, I think Gonzalo García is a proper player and will shine over the course of the season.

Palace, I think, are paying the price for the January splurge on Brennan Johnson and Jorgen Strand Larsen, not just the inflated fees but the sizeable wages on players who contributed almost nothing. I was at Leeds vs Brentford last week and there was plenty to admire about both sides but fear for Leeds’ so-far commendable resilience at their Amex knacker’s yard and wonder whether Sunderland will be able to live with Brentford’s pace. Manchester City vs Coventry, meanwhile, probably will not give us the Bouaddi-Fernández-Anderson £325m midfield from the start but we might be given a glimpse.

#37864. Latest Update: Thomas Tuchel is now embracing traditional English values - clarity has helped England understand who they are, and now they can beat the best, writes CRAIG HOPE

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (926 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Thomas Tuchel is now embracing traditional English values - clarity has helped England understand who they are, and now they can beat the best, writes CRAIG HOPE

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 16:57 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 16:57 EST, 16 November 2026.
  • Thomas Tuchel has always liked what he sees from his England players on the training pitch.
  • It is why, when the squad reconvened at St George’s Park in September, Tuchel used the meeting room as much as he did the grass to address that disparity in delivery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 16:57 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 16:57 EST, 16 November 2026.

Thomas Tuchel has always liked what he sees from his England players on the training pitch. Less so, at times, inside a stadium. It is a contradiction with which he has wrestled since the World Cup, when performances on the whole left him underwhelmed, save for the collective spirit and individual excellence that rescued results.

It is why, when the squad reconvened at St George’s Park in September, Tuchel used the meeting room as much as he did the grass to address that disparity in delivery.

At the same time, the elephant in the corner of the auditorium was the German’s own comments about the DNA of English players compared to the likes of Spain, and fundamentally them lacking the coding to protect possession and, therefore, valuable leads. He asked Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and others for their thoughts.

In a recent development, the message back from his players was this – let us be better at being us, not them. Interestingly, that was Tuchel’s mantra upon his appointment, one of embracing traditional English values. Amid the World Cup fallout, though, he had wandered in a daze down a rabbit hole of genetics, focusing on what his team cannot do as opposed to what they can.

Tuchel, his staff and his players are tacticians and technicians, not scientists. If the intricacies of DNA do not allow them to be Spain, then don’t be. Be England, they determined. That is not to say kick and rush, bark and bite. After all, Kane is officially the best player in the world right now and Bellingham, unofficially, is playing as well as anyone on the planet.

Rather, there needed to be clarity – this is what we are and this is how we beat the best. On Sunday night in Madrid, England beat the very best. It was a victory born from those hours on the training field and in conference, and even more spent by Tuchel and his assistant Anthony Barry during their post-tournament review in a St George’s Park war room. They knew then that this was not a case of rip it up and start again, more so mend the tears and give the likes of Bellingham a blank sheet to impact where, and how, he sees best.

Thomas Tuchel is embracing England's DNA and reaping the rewards following the World Cup.

England can now beat the best, which they indicated against Spain in a fantastic victory.

In a recent development, there was no radical strategical change, but there was a fresh doctrine, principles that should underpin whatever the in-game circumstance – off-the-ball running, a high press, filling in for a team-mate who has seized a moment to improvise elsewhere, such as the full backs. Ben White scoring England’s third on Sunday and Lewis Hall completing four more dribbles than Lamine Yamal were examples of Tuchel’s allowance for greater intuition. Be you, not Spain.

According to recent reports, kane, informally at least, has also been promoted beyond captain, a bridge between management and dressing-room. To see him in a semi-coaching and cajoling capacity on the touchline after he was taken off in the 78th minute against Spain was to witness this elevation.

But even if England had conceded a late equaliser at the Metropolitano Stadium, it would not have mattered. Not when it comes to measuring post World Cup improvement. To have drawn comparison with Argentina and that second-half collapse would have been unfair and inaccurate. The semi-final was 11 versus 11 and so let us judge this game on the same terms. And what did England do with a 1-0 lead and 11 players? They attacked. And attacked again. For all of the tweaks Tuchel and Barry have made to the structure of training and the team’s set-up, this was evidence of them learning from a mistake, as much as the head coach will be loath to admit.

Ezri Konsa, however, did reveal there was a definite instruction to keep attacking Spain when Tuchel addressed the team at half-time.

‘The instruction was to keep going at them,’ remarked the defender. ‘Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. That is what we did. Argentina was different, different circumstances. But it was not just half-time. We went 1-0 up and Harry, our captain, told us to keep going and to keep our foot on the pedal too.'.

In a recent development, before Jarell Quansah’s needless mistake and Elliot Anderson’s subsequent dismissal in the 63rd minute, the game was not in the balance in any way. As a live observer of almost every Tuchel match since his arrival, this was the best performance of his reign. In fact, it’s not even close.

Sources indicate that and yet, so much still comes back to Bellingham. England would not have won without him. He terrified Spain, perhaps given their intimate knowledge of his powers. Beating the best is as much a mental challenge as it is physical, and Bellingham believed. He made England believe, too. His swagger. His majesty. And yes, his skill. He won the corner for Konsa’s headed second and created the third for White. He then dropped into midfield when down to ten and battled and organised like a captain.

Bellingham has bought into the collective under Tuchel and, with that, his team-mates are buying into his massive ideas. For now, they don’t come much bigger than what England achieved in Madrid.

And if Leeds United are performing and carrying themselves like an established Premier League team, perhaps it is time to start treating them as one.

A growing number of pundits are viewing Leeds in those terms after being impressed by the way the club have taken to life back in the top flight.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Industry observers note that united's physicality and intensity have marked them out as one of the hardest teams to beat. They have lost just seven league games since the start of 2026, while their defence ranks among the best in the division this season – an improvement underpinned by summer signings James Trafford and Tarik Muharemovic.

Farke himself feels his players have done enough to earn the respect of pundits, although he has cautioned them against believing the hype.

"It's a credit to our work in the last years," he said. "I would also agree, based on our performances, that we deserve a bit the label and praise.

"But we also don't go into the trap where we think that we are already the finished product or better than we are. We know that we have to fight for each and every point because other clubs are more established.

"We have an unbelievable tradition and are a huge club in the UK. Everyone knows that this club belongs at the top level.

In a recent development, "We have a clear vision for our short, mid-term and long-term but it's also fair to say that in the last 25 years we haven't spent too many years at the Premier League level. Our best finish in that time is exactly one top-half finish in position nine.

Industry observers note that "For that, we don't go into the trap and believe all the praise. We know that we are good and are not doubting ourselves too much; we play with confidence.

In a recent development, "But we don't go into the trap of thinking that we can win games with even 95 per cent effort. We're still a side in our second year after promotion and have to show some craft and fight in order to become an established Premier League side.".

Chelsea provide another measure of Leeds' progress today, the first of three challenging away assignments before Christmas.

Farke, whose side travel to Manchester City and Liverpool in early December, is bidding to become the first United manager to mastermind a win at Stamford Bridge since David O'Leary in 1999.

"I know it's a while ago since we travelled away from Stamford Bridge with three points," stated Farke.

"It will be difficult but if we are at our very best, we also know we're capable of winning points wherever we go. We have to make sure we are on it.

In a recent development, "The preparations have been difficult this week but it's also very similar for Chelsea. We're looking forward to this game.".

Leeds return from the international break hoping to build on their impressive victory over in-form Tottenham Hotspur.

Chelsea, meanwhile, are looking to respond to their disappointing defeat at Sunderland last time out.

Xabi Alonso's side have shown their attacking potential in flashes – not least when they hammered Leeds 6-3 in the League Cup – but a record of five wins, four defeats and a solitary draw in the league hints at a team still finding their way under the fresh manager.

Farke, however, has warned his players not to read too much into Chelsea's inconsistency.

"I expect top-class players and also a top manager," he remarked.

Sources indicate that "It's no secret that they have world-class potential in their squad. That's why they've spent so much money in the last years – to build a squad with unbelievable individual quality, especially up front.

Recent findings suggest that "It's difficult. It's never guaranteed that if you have so many quality players that you play each and every opponent out of the park.

In a recent development, "Some of their last opponents have made their life difficult but it's still important to be aware of their quality and strength. We have to make sure we don't allow them to develop that strength.

"It's also key that we take part in this game in terms of having as much possession as possible and that we also dominate the ball because when they have the ball, they have so much talent, skill and potential to make something happen.

"For Leeds United, it's always a bit of a special fixture to travel to London and play Chelsea. We are very respectful but definitely not fearful.".

Leeds took four points off the Blues last season on their way to a 14th-place finish.

They have made an encouraging start to their second campaign back at the top level but Farke is staying grounded.

The Leeds boss expects the coming weeks to offer a clearer indication of how the table is shaping up as clubs brace themselves for a long, uninterrupted run of fixtures.

Industry observers note that "Until November, it's the starting period of the Premier League," said Farke. "It's key to put yourselves into a good position. We have done this with good performances and are sitting on 14 points in the top half of the table.

According to recent reports, "There will be many, many games and challenges due to workloads, injuries, illnesses and perhaps suspensions. For that, it's not the moment to be too carried away. It's a period where we have to be really on it and fight for everything.

Industry observers note that "After this period, we can have a look and see where we are in the table for the run-in. This upcoming month is quite important for the final table.".

“In the last few hours, Barcelona’s sporting director Deco spoke about Alejandro Balde and said that they are not planning on Balde’s exit because we are only in mid-November; there is a month and a half to go until January.

“Barça play every two or three days and a player like Balde can clearly still be useful between now and the transfer market. It’s true that Barça has left-back cover at the moment, but Barça doesn’t want to put a player like Balde on the market publicly already in mid-November.

“The reality behind the scenes is different: Balde remains a player who could leave in January, because Jorge Mendes, the player’s agent, was in Barcelona this week to speak with the player and discuss a strategy.

“Balde could therefore leave, but we must be realistic because there are significant figures at stake, given that he earns more than €5 million net and in the summer Barcelona were asking for €50 million for him.

“We’ll see if the formula can change in January, but on the one hand, Deco says so, on the other, there’s the reality: if Balde doesn’t play as well as he hasn’t been playing between now and January, the idea of ​​Balde leaving could become concrete.

“We told you that he’s right now being offered to Roma, but the Giallorossi haven’t really picked up steam yet. They’ve also offered him to Milan; the player was initially proposed last summer, but without a transfer, nothing happened.

“We’ll see what happens with Alejandro Balde, but he’s a name for the international or possibly Italian market that we need to keep there.”.

In a recent development, the Scottish Premiership match between Celtic and St Mirren takes place at Celtic Park, Glasgow on Saturday, November 21, 2026. Kick-off is 3pm.

According to recent reports, the match has not been selected for live TV coverage in the UK. Highlights will be shown on Sportscene on BBC One Scotland at 10.20pm.

Auston Trusty is back for Celtic after a family bereavement, but Mika Baur faces 10 weeks out with an ankle injury and Alistair Johnston (hamstring) is yet to return. Benjamin Nygren (heel) is a doubt and Joel van den Berg picked up a knock earlier in the week.

St Mirren midfielders Ryan Carr and Paul Nsio return, while Ismeal Kabia (calf), Nikolas Agrafiotis (calf), Keanu Baccus (Achilles), Malik Dijksteel (hamstring) and Jonah Ayunga (knee) remain out.

Recent findings suggest that matthew MacDermid is the match referee. Chris Rae and Ross Anderson are serving as the assistant referees, while Graham Grainger is the fourth official. Greg Aitken is in the VAR room, assisted by Ross Hardie.

Head coach Fabian Hurzeler admits it was not always easy for Brajan Gruda at Brighton.

Gruda joined Brighton in 2024 for £25m from Bundesliga club Mainz and indicated glimpses of his potential with the Seagulls.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The German playmaker made 43 appearances and claimed four goals with eight assists but struggled to nail down a regular starting position.

Right wing and the No 10 spot is Gruda's preferred role and he was regularly behind the likes of Yankuba Minteh, Diego Gomez and Georginio Rutter in the pecking order.

Gruda joined RB Leipzig on loan for the second part of last term and then agreed to a season-long loan last summer.

The 22-year-old has impressed in the Bundesliga and has five goals and eight assists in total for Martín Demichelis' Leipzig, who are fourth in the German top flight.

Gruda also dazzled for Germany last week as he scored a fine individual goal on his full debut against Serbia and then claimed two assists and netted a goal in Germany's 5-0 win against The Netherlands. Brighton's Bart Verbruggen was in goal for the Dutch.

Germany boss Jurgen Klopp heaped praise on Gruda. "He's a fantastic player who loves to take people on," mentioned the former Liverpool manager. "And he hasn't yet fulfilled his potential.".

Gruda is contracted with Brighton until 2028 and his loan at Liepzig is believed to have an obligation to buy, with certain conditions.

Recent findings suggest that “The obligation to buy for Brajan Gruda will be activated in 2027 due to accounting reasons," posted German transfer expert Florian Plettenberg. "The total package for RB Leipzig will amount to €30m.".

He also stated that Bayern Munich are keeping a close eye on the situation.

Gruda's development has left many Brighton fans hoping for a return - especially with the uncertainty surrounding Minteh, who almost joined Liverpool last summer.

"I'm also full of praise for Gruda," remarked Fabian Hurzeler to Sussex World ahead Sunday's trip to Hull City.

"Because when I see him playing, I see a great development. He's doing the basic things well. I think one thing that Jürgen always mentioned is to make him run back, to make him defend.

"I think this will always be the key for his game. Then in possession, he always has the quality to beat an opponent.".

It has been revealed that asked why it did not work out for him at Brighton, Hurzeler told Sussex World: "Again, he was very young with us. For us, it was always important to give him more game minutes.

"He had a lot of competition when Minteh was playing in this position, Diego Gomez was in this position. So it was not that easy for him to get those game minutes.

"Then he made the move to Leipzig, where he had more and more game minutes.

"Especially with these young players, I think you see brilliantly now with our young players, if they get game minutes, if they have this trust and confidence, then they are capable of doing really good things.

"I think that was the only glitch here with him, that he didn't have this confidence and these game minutes, and now he can really express himself.".

Sources indicate that hurzeler is though delighted by his improvement and believes working with Klopp is a "good fit" for Gruda. The Brighton boss was however coy on whether Gruda will be seen in Brighton colours again.

"It's a joy to watch him,” he noted to Sussex World. “I'm really happy to see him playing like this. I think it's a good fit with Jürgen.

"I think that Jürgen really gets this belief into his players and therefore it was a joy to watch Germany playing this week.

"To see them chasing as a team, to see them doing counter-pressing, gegenpressing, and that's really good.

"I'm really happy for Brajan, so let's see how the future will be.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last season, Hull won promotion via the Championship play-offs on the back of a squad who has been the course and distance in the division.

That group was put together under restrictions which stopped Hull buying or even paying a loan fee for players in 2025-26. With the restrictions lifted and a ticket for the gravy train that is the world's most lucrative domestic football league, they have broadened their horizons.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Eighteen players were signed – although Joe Gelhardt was a loan made permanent – and are overwhelmingly young and newly introduced to English football.

Yet according to 22-year-old Cho – who spent his childhood flitting between England and France – as well as performing brilliantly in the season’s first ten games, the old guard have welcomed the next generation.

According to recent reports, it is why Hull go into Sunday's Premier League game at home to Brighton and Hove Albion still unbeaten on the banks of the Humber this season. Whoever pulled on the black and amber, the Tigers simply would not be able to compete if their squad was fractured.

"The lads that were here before, they've been amazing with the fresh lads," claims the French-born player in an English accent which shows why he has represented both countries in international age-group football.

"We've been settling in really well.

It has been revealed that "I don't think there's two groups. Everyone's joking with everyone, everyone's working with everyone.

"It does say a lot (about the mainly British and Irish players who were at the club last season). Then again, it's football and we're at a high level, so everyone knows there's going to be a lot of competition.

"The main thing is just being as good as you can to each other off the pitch and then when we're on the pitch as competitive as possible.

Industry observers note that "I feel that's a really crucial strength because that's what's got us here so far. I feel like we need to keep that until the end of the season.".

Not all of the new signings came speaking good English, so Cho's bilingualism is notable.

According to recent reports, "I've got a few of the French players I'm pretty close to," he indicates. "Lucas Gourna (a team-mate in the French age-group teams) speaks fairly good English so it's not too much of a problem with him.

"But Nobel (Mendy) and Robinio (Vaz), they don't speak that good English so sometimes you have to help them out.

"I've got my family not too far from here in Manchester so that's been really helpful, and some of my team-mates live really close by so we always go to each other's (homes) and just chill with each other.

"It's really important off the pitch what you do to be good on the pitch.".

If Cho's off-field role is clear, on the field it has been less so.

He may not have had the language barrier to hurdle, but he has had many of the problems his team-mates did joining late in the transfer window, in his case because of what he calls a "roller-coaster" of an on-off transfer. Coach Sergej Jakirovic thinks he has still not yet caught up.

"He's a very quick player so he can run behind," explains Jakirovic. "Maybe sometimes he can better cover the ball, to save the ball (keep possession), at least to win a foul.

"It's also about fitness because his recovery after sprinting is still too long. In his last club (Nice), he was removed from training because he was waiting for a transfer. Ten days he didn't train with the team.

"Now he's healthy, thank God, and everything's on him (to perform).".

It has been revealed that hull have largely used Cho from the bench as a right winger but their best player, Mohamed Belloumi – one of the younger members of the old guard – plays there too. Their next best, Oli McBurnie, is a centre-forward, his other position.

So it was significant for Cho that Jakirovic switched from 5-4-1 to 5-3-2 at Arsenal, giving Cho a first Premier League start alongside McBurnie.

"I need to keep working and stay ready," claims Cho, who picked up a minor injury on the back of his first goal. "Wherever the coach wants me to play, I'm just trying to be as helpful as I can to the team.

"(Arsenal) was a great experience. I knew it was going to be tough even before the game.

"But Iit was just trying to make advantage of my colleagues by getting in behind, trying to hurt the opponents with my runs in behind and trying to be a threat every time we had the ball in transition.

"I know I can do better, we can do better as a team always but I feel like there's a lot to take from it.".

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Andy Robertson admitted Scotland don’t have time to get things right under Sebastien Pocognoli after the team were humbled by Switzerland on the night of the skipper’s record 103rd cap.

John McGinn warned this week it could take the Scots up to 18 months to fully grasp the Belgian’s tactical aims.

But serious questions are now being asked of Pocognoli after his team were swept aside in a miserable 4-0 defeat to a much-changed Swiss side.

The result, combined with Slovenia’s 3-0 win over North Macedonia, ended Scotland’s already scant hopes of a Nations League promotion play-off spot and condemned them to pot three in next month’s Euro 2028 draw.

Robertson was hoping for a night to remember as he overtook Kenny Dalglish as the country’s most capped player but was clearly furious as the Scots crumbled in St Gallen.

Asked if it was going to take time for things to click under Pocognoli, he told the BBC: ‘I don’t think you’ve got time in international football, you have to do it.

Scotland skipper Andy Robertson laments a night to forget on the occasion of his 103rd cap.

‘These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

‘We don’t have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.

‘We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow.

‘We really need to step up again. In international football, you do not have time.’.

After an unconvincing start to his reign, Pocognoli needed a statement victory to convince sceptical fans that he is the right man for the job.

Despite a promising start, the rot set in after Lewis Ferguson’s 22nd minute own-goal.

The Swiss, missing a host of key players, went further ahead with goals from Winsley Boteli, Alvyn Sanches and Zeki Amdouni.

Almost 12 months on from the famous night when Steve Clarke’s side beat Denmark to reach the World Cup, the Tartan Army will be looking towards the European qualifiers with trepidation.

Robertson is tackled by Switzerland's Zachary Athekame on a night of few positives.

Industry observers note that robertson said: ‘First half, I thought we were in the game. We lost a stupid goal but I thought we had chances and it could have been 2-1 at half-time.

‘By the time you get to 50 minutes and you are 3-0 down, that can’t happen in international football.

‘We were playing a good team but I felt we were in the game, it is a really tough night for us.’.

Pocognoli also felt the final scoreline was harsh and rued his side’s inability to make the most of the opportunities they created.

‘The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don’t think it’s a reflection of the game, if I’m really honest and objective,’ said Pocognoli.

In a recent development, ‘I think we had some very good moments, we started like we wanted, aggressive away from home. I think we played a good first half, we created chances, we were dominant in some moments and we faced Switzerland with different shapes and adapted well from the first minute.

Sebastien Pocognoli will now face some searching questions over his suitability for the job.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I think we conceded the goal from maybe one of the first chances they had. We also created chances but we were not clinical in that moment in the box.

‘In the second half, yeah, we started poorly from the first minute, a poor corner we gave away. Then you feel that, OK, we will get punished.

‘But I think when we made the substitutions, they made an impact, and we should have scored two goals in that period.

‘At the end, it’s a bad feeling, the score, but I think that the players try to do their best and create moments that we want to see.’.

It takes the Reds to within three points from safety, with as many games in hand against 22nd-placed Rochdale.

Reds made a fast start to the first half and took the lead in the fourth minute through Jennings, following Kellan Gordon’s cross from a darting run down the right wing.

Fleetwood, Arsenal’s conquerors and League Cup quarter-finalists, failed to clear their lines on the edge of the six-yard box and Jennings pounced on their indecision to smash home into the roof of the net.

New Reds centre back Ben Heneghan blocked a well-hit shot from range in the Cod Army’s first effort on goal in the ninth minute.

Vito Mannone calmy claimed Jake Batty’s left-wing cross to dispel Fleetwood as the away side got a foothold in the game and started to up the pressure, shortly before Reds nervily dealt with an Andy Cannon cross.

Dylan Mogan nearly put the Reds 2-0 up on the half hour, he tricked his way past the Fleetwood right-back but curling shot from the edge of the box clipped the post and went out for a goal kick.

Just before the break Fleetwood’s Aaron Loupal-Bi got into a good position on the left after a one-two but his tame effort along the ground was collected by Mannone.

Reds flew out the traps to double their lead within a minute of the restart, Morgan stormed through Fleetwood’s midfield and slotted Aderoju in on-goal and the massive target man rifled a left-foot shot into the back of the net.

Fleetwood gave themselves a lifeline thanks to substitute Will Davies’ firing a shot past Mannone from the middle of the penalty area to give the travelling fans behind the goal a reason to cheer.

Reds matched Fleetwood as the physicality grew as the half wore on and dug in to match their opponents.

Fleetwood substitute Lewis McCann stung the gloves of Mannone and produced a match-winning save from the significant Italian who’s clean sheet was hard-earned.

Duke-McKenna had the chance to seal the points for the Reds at the end after chopping back onto his left foot down the right side, but his curled shot was parried away by Lynch.

Celtic manager Martin O’Neill hopes Luke McCowan’s performance in the 4-1 win over St Mirren can be a catalyst to reignite his Parkhead career.

O’Neill watched his side open up a seven-point gap on second-placed Rangers, who face Motherwell on Saturday evening, blowing away St Mirren before half-time thanks to goals from Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain (33), Camilo Duran (40) and McCowan (42). Callum McGregor (63) added a fourth, with Killian Phillips (69) scoring a consolation penalty for the away side.

Dealt a double blow ahead of the game, midfield pair Benjamin Nygren and Mika Baur both ruled out after picking up injuries on international duty, O’Neill handed McCowan his first start in over two months in the centre of the park alongside Oxlade-Chamberlain.

Sources indicate that mcCowan has suffered in the last few months, dropping out of the matchday squad after a high-profile error in the defeat to LASK during the Champions League playoffs. Forced to delete his Instagram account to escape personal abuse from sections of the online support, the former Dundee captain had played just 14 minutes since being hauled off at half-time in a 1-0 home defeat to Rangers on September 20.

“I thought he did really well for us,” was O’Neill’s assessment of McCowan’s return to the starting line-up. “It was his first full game for a considerable amount of time. He got the ball once and he played it almost blindly and it was intercepted and I thought ‘oh gosh, here we go’. But he roared back. Took the goal great, and I’m really pleased for him because he’s a really genuine lad.

“It has been tough [for him]. I thought in the game against Rangers, he was thrown into position, and it didn’t start well for him in the match. I thought it felt like deja vu for him after his last game against Rangers at the back end of last season, too. For him today, I felt that was a big boost for him. I’m pleased that there’s a bit of competition for places [in midfield] now. Which is good. But I am pleased that him and Alex got on the field and were able to play. That itself is a confidence booster.”.

In a recent development, duran had the ball in the net for Celtic after five minutes but assistant referee signalled for an offside. The home side thought they’d taken the lead again just after the quarter hour mark, with Duran the disappointed party once more. Blasting home the rebound after Jota’s shot was parried away by Jacob Chapman, the frustrated Colombian looked to sky as the flag went up for offside in the build up for a second time.

A misplaced pass from McCowan signalled a groan from the home crowd as Celtic frustration crept in, however, they needn’t have worried, finding their opener via Oxlade-Chamberlain just after the half-hour mark, with the experienced midfielder slamming home from close range after a positive forward run and cross from Hyun-Jun Yang on the right-wing.

It has been revealed that it was no less than the home side deserved, but the momentary VAR check for the opener followed by a blocked goal-bound effort from Killian Phillips offered some unexpected anxiety in the immediate aftermath. O’Neill’s side added further unnecessary stress on a bitterly cold Glasgow afternoon when Yang somehow failed to square to Duran when clean through on goal.

The striker finally got on the scoresheet with a fine header shortly before the break.

A moment of redemption followed just 120 seconds later when the returning McCowan collected a neat cut back from Jota in the area to fire home first time beyond Chapman, effectively killing the game before the break.

It has been revealed that his first goal since the 5-1 win over Kilmarnock on August 9, a relatively muted celebration followed from McCowan as he was congratulated by his teammates. Virtually out of the picture at Celtic in recent weeks, he’ll hope it’s not his last and that his unexpected reprieve can lead to an extended spell in his boyhood club’s engine room. The victory already wrapped up in nine first-half minutes, McGregor’s placed shot added to the scoreline just after the hour mark, with Phillips’ penalty after a foul from goalkeeper Sam Johnstone on Calvin Ramsay in the box just a consolation.

Recent findings suggest that O’Neill also addressed the omission of Haissem Hassan during his press-match conference and the fitness of Baur and Alistair Johnston. Quashing rumours that the Egyptian was left out against Kilmarnock prior to the international break because he was “unpopular” within the squad earlier this week, the 74-year-old has insisted that both Hassan and Kasper Hogh, who was an unused substitute, will have a part to play against Torreense in the Europa League on Thursday night.

“Kasper will be ready for Thursday,” remarked O’Neill. “That’s the point. We’re going to need him on Thursday. For want of a better word, it’s more rotation than anything else. Kasper is fine. He’ll [Haissem] will be there for Thursday as well. He’s missed a couple of games. He didn’t come back until Friday from the international break, a couple of them didn’t.

“We were worried about Duran after he travelled halfway around the world, but he was amazing in training.

In a recent development, “Baur is in a boot. If that injury stretches to end of January, we’ll think about making a change [to the Europa League squad]. Alistair was getting a scan and some treatment this weekend in Dublin. We’ll find out about that and get an upgrade. I’m hoping it’s going to be good news. He’s feeling decent within himself now.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a night dedicated to Weston Park's cancer work, the Reds extended that charity to their defending, and within 15 minutes, Wednesday already looked uncatchable.

Vimal Yoganathan's sixth goal in eight games ensured a proper South Yorkshire derby broke out, but the Reds are getting rather too good at nearly or semi-performances for their own comfort down in the League One relegation zone.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

After Yoganathan's strike, the home side revealed the fight they should be a given in games against the near-neighbours, but it was already too late.

For the visitors, it was a character test passed in front of 5,700 invigilators in the away end, Jamal Lowe scoring from their only two shots on target on a night that felt like a big step forward for their latest manager, Dave Challinor.

"Three points away ole, ole," sang the packed away end and more pertinently, "Wednesday are back.".

Funny how one week can totally change the mood of a football club.

The Reds actually started the better, but they are getting good at looking good in ineffectual parts of the field, and awful at the business ends.

Their fans had been in mutinous mood before the game, hundreds gathering outside the ground before kick-off to protest about the way things are being run, but there was no such defiance when they needed it early on.

Lowe – playing more of an orthodox winger role with the balance of Wednesday's unchanged side titled more towards a back four than a three than it had been the previous week – was ruthless in exploiting it.

When Barry Bannan lofted a free-kick to the back post in the ninth minute, Liam Cooper was in far too much space there. The defender headed the ball across goal, and Lowe pounced for the Owls' third set-piece goal in a week.

Five minutes later, two passes took the visitors from the halfway line to a second goal.

Callum Slattery's pass to Bannan was almost cut out but when he found Lowe, but Jubril Okedina stood off, almost daring the forward to score, so he did.

Barnsley's early work lacked that conviction.

In a recent development, reyes Cleary's second-minute snapshot lacked the power to beat Joe Lumley, and Ryan Brownlie's also allowed the goalkeeper to save. Makenzie Kirk miskicked a shot when Cleary picked him out, and when Patrick Kelly ran onto a knockdown by the centre-forward, his shot lacked power.

Cleary put a shot well wide and Luca Connell hammered one into Billy Mitchell.

Ziyad Larkeche controlled a fairly routine Cieran Slicker pass over the touchline.

But a side with seven starters under the age of 23 plugged away and got back into it courtesy of one of their young leaders.

Like Okedina, Yan Valery stood off Cleary and when the winger delivered a low cross, Yoganathan arrived onto it like a centre-forward to pull a goal back.

With both sides attacking their own noisy ends, it made for an entertaining second half.

Like Barnsley at the start of the first half, Wednesday pushed the harder, without making it count.

Bannan had a shot blocked and when Slicker came out of his goal to stop former Red Davis Keillor-Dunn finishing a Bannan pass, Lowe lifted his shot onto the roof of the net.

At the other end, Barnsley centre-back Sam Gale forced his way to the byline, but his cross cleared those in the area. Larkeche put an acrobatic effort wide.

It was Wednesday who were throwing on the substitutes - a sign of their deeper resources, but also off their keenness to finally add to Lowe's second shot on target, 14 minutes in.

Despite one of those substitutes, Harry Gray, accelerating past Gale for a chance Slattery had blocked, it never came, but it did not need to because hard as Barnsley pushed – throwing centre-back Connor O'Riordan on as a late emergency striker and sending Slicker up for a stoppage-time corner – they could not find the next goal either.

Luca Connell came the closest, his free-kick tipped over in the 93rd minute.

It has been revealed that his team are just not good enough to gift promotion wannabes like Wednesday a two-goal headstart and get away with it. Only just, you might say, but game after game that is enough.

Barnsley: Slicker; Okedina (Reid 86), Gale, Kay, Larkeche; Connell, Kelly (Johnson 86); Brownlie (O'Riordan 90), Yoganathan (Noslin 81), Cleary; Kirk (Toure 81).

Unused substitutes: Ravenhill, Alker.

Sheffield Wednesday: Lumley; Valery, Bernard (Santos 86), Cooper, Swinkels (Palmer 70); Heskey, Mitchell (Barry 70), Slattery, Bannan (Gray 78), J Lowe (Liongola 70); Keillor-Dunn.

Unused substitutes: Morrison, Trueman.

Referee: O Yates (Staffordshire).

Industry News: Arsenal teach Chelsea a lesson in how to be champions

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is how champions are supposed to play and, although the Arsenal home support have not seen a team defend their place at the apex of English league football for two decades, they knew it when they saw it.
  • The chase was on for Mikel Arteta’s team within two minutes when Morgan Rogers, the man who might have moved to Arsenal this summer, put his latest club Chelsea in the lead.
  • Industry observers note that others might have crumbled.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is how champions are supposed to play and, although the Arsenal home support have not seen a team defend their place at the apex of English league football for two decades, they knew it when they saw it.

The chase was on for Mikel Arteta’s team within two minutes when Morgan Rogers, the man who might have moved to Arsenal this summer, put his latest club Chelsea in the lead. So unfolded a thrilling 100 minutes of Premier League competition. Arsenal were the better team in terms of ambition and attack even if one could not discount Chelsea until the very last moment.

Industry observers note that others might have crumbled. That Chelsea did not will give Xabi Alonso hope for a team that did not feature the injured Moisés Caicedo and is now without the departed Enzo Fernández. Yet he will also recognise that his childhood friend from San Sebastián in the other dugout has created a side that treated the game, and their place in it, with an urgency that looks different. The first two minutes might have been ragged for Arsenal but after that they did not let the game happen to them.

Morgan Rogers fires Chelsea in front inside TWO minutes! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/ca8cqnT2Wm.

Instead, Arteta’s players drove this contest, and the sequence of chances that came and went was dizzying at times. Their best players scored the two goals. First Kai Havertz, who now has three in four games this season, and then the captain Martin Ødegaard who dispatched what would be the winner.

"A spear through the heart of Chelsea!" Martin Odegaard puts Arsenal in front at the Emirates 🎯 pic.twitter.com/5deEQykjck.

Ødegaard looked like the veteran of a title-winning season, and a deep run in the World Cup – an accomplished, shrewd performer in a midfield that was fought over ferociously all afternoon.

Sources indicate that as for the game’s defining moment – it would be hard to overlook the feint from Havertz for the winning goal. It deceived the Chelsea players around him and created the channel for Christos Tzolis’s cross to reach Ødegaard. His goal was a close copy, in style and personnel, of the one he scored against Manchester City in the Community Shield but it was crowned by Havertz’s bluff. He shaped to take the ball and let it run under his foot at the last moment.

Sources indicate that this was Chelsea’s first defeat in three – leaving only Arsenal and City with nine points from their first three games – although the seven goals conceded is the standout. For all the jet fuel in their attack they keep conceding. This was a much more exacting test than Fulham and Brighton previously, but even so. Alonso has introduced his preferred back three, often a back five, and it is a work in progress.

Arsenal have set the standard in that regard and they were uncompromising again. They did not replicate the errors that led to the Rogers goal and they pushed the limits at all times. Gabriel Magalhães kicked Emi Martínez in the head competing for a ball in the Chelsea area. Myles Lewis-Skelly went after João Pedro. Ben White and Roméo Lavia saw things differently in the first half. This Arsenal team does not shy away from those confrontations in the way their predecessors often did.

In fact, it was notable just how furiously Rogers reacted to Declan Rice when the two England team-mates converged as the Chelsea man charged off to join a late counter-attack. The bad feeling lingered even after the game when Rogers seemed unwilling to forgive. Rice had applied the minimum contact and the maximum cynicism to stop Rogers while the attention of referee Chris Kavanagh was elsewhere.

"He's FUMING Morgan Rogers!" 😳 pic.twitter.com/FciivEedvh.

Recent findings suggest that all that ringcraft was one thing, but it should be mentioned that Arsenal were excellent in setting an attacking tempo that will be hell for any team to live with – especially at the Emirates. Havertz is now Arteta’s centre-forward of choice in the absence of a major summer acquisition. Viktor Gyökeres made a late substitute’s appearance – his first minutes of the season. The hierarchy is clear: last season’s great goalscoring hope is now back-up.

Sources indicate that “Exceptional” was how Arteta described his team’s response to the early Rogers goal. They had twice failed to clear the ball in their own area when first Maxence Lacroix and then Jorrel Hato created the chance. Rogers’s right foot half-volley was not struck on the full, but it was placed perfectly inside the post with the necessary bounce and skip to mean David Raya never got behind it.

In a recent development, arteta’s squad runs deep enough that in the closing stages he could relieve his midfield with two Spanish World Cup-winning substitutes – Martín Zubimendi and Mikel Merino. Then there was Noni Madueke on for Bukayo Saka, understudy and first-choice for club and country. This was not Saka’s day in the way it has been in the past, although a very promising shot of his was stopped by Martinez in the first half.

In a recent development, in the pounding that Chelsea took after they went into the lead, Riccardo Calafiori had an equaliser within minutes that was disallowed by VAR on an offside call. The left-back was the third in sequence to try to force the ball over the line from a Rice free-kick. Calafiori was successful, but the second of his team-mates to try, Ezri Konsa, had been offside when he connected.

For the equaliser it was Havertz, accelerating cautiously at first and then full-on with his left foot from the right-side. Ødegaard was well-placed to prevent Lacroix getting close but in truth the challenge never had the force required. Havertz’s shot was not totally convincing but then neither was Martinez’s attempt to save it – every bit as uncertain as Raya for the Chelsea goal.

A precise finish from Kai Havertz and Arsenal are level! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/DqL1MEX4zN.

Chelsea had profited from the quick ball out to their right where Calafiori was often out of position in the left-back slot and Pedro Neto could cut in on his left foot. That seemed to be the sacrifice that Arteta was prepared to make in keeping the hammer on Chelsea. If Neto had not struck the post in one such escape in time added on at the end of the first half it might have been different.

Ødegaard struck what would be the winner early in the first half, and although Chelsea fizzed enough in the later stages it always felt as though it was Arsenal’s game. Raya came into his own in the 89th minute when Estêvão, a substitute, cut in from the right and hit a fierce shot that the goalkeeper pushed over. It was close in some ways – and in others not at all.

“It hurts. It hurts because a defeat has to hurt. It has been a very intense game with different moments for everything. We had chances to equalise. In the first half as well a couple of chances. Never happy if you lose.

“After we scored, there were 15-20 minutes where we had to defend too much and we were struggling a bit to get control. We then had better spells with the ball. Overall, it was a very tight, very intense game. We could do better with the second goal to conceded too early. The guys gave everything, tried everything. It has to hurt.

“It is about preparing the best possible way to compete the best possible way. You need to control the overloads on the right side. It is part of the game to have these actions. We continue. It is game three and this is going to be a long, long ride.”.

"That's not sustainable" Daniel Sturridge reflects Chelsea's performance after the 2-1 defeat to Arsenal 💭 pic.twitter.com/3EMx88QLA0.

"He's not the goalkeeper that won the World Cup" 🏆Jamie Carragher indicates Emi Martinez is not as quick or sharp as he once was 🧤 pic.twitter.com/SOp4XhoYIr.

Recent findings suggest that “I think the worrying thing for everybody else already is that [William] Saliba, who is genuinely world-class arguably, probably the best centre-back in world football, has not played a minute of football so far this season. And it does not look like anyone can score against them.

“There is a massive gulf between both teams; their XIs and the squads. It will take Chelsea a while to get to that level, if they can get there. But I thought Arsenal were fantastic today. We do not normally see Arsenal in these games, end-to-end, because they very rarely go behind. They are so strong defensively they do not need to get involved in those games.

“They still did not look like they were going to give too much away, even though they were bombing forwards and putting so many bodies in the opposition box.”.

It has been revealed that “It was a massive game with a tough opponent. It was really hard for us; we got there in the end. Our mentality is to keep fighting. Conceding early was not ideal but we reacted really well. We played well in the second half and got our reward. We showed our quality today. The result reflected that.”.

On his relationship with Kai Havertz:.

In a recent development, “He is a really smart player and moves so well. He takes defenders attention. When he makes the run and I come from behind I am always free. It was a brilliant goal.”.

“We knew Arsenal were the better team and they have proven that in this game. The question before today was, how close are Chelsea? And [Xabi] Alonso will be proud of what he has seen. There are obviously improvements to be made, but they gave it a right good go. A lot of very good things and they will be frustrated and disappointed, but they may potentially look back on this game as a good moment rather than as bad as it may feel right now.”.

Switzerland 4-0 Scotland: Swiss stroll leaves serious question marks over Sebastien Pocognoli as Scots round off miserable campaign with defeat on captain Andrew Robertson's record-breaking night

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 17:06 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 18:08 EST, 16 November 2026.
  • Despite re-establishing Scotland’s credentials as a credible football nation, by common consent, Steve Clarke’s time in charge of the side was up in the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:06 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 18:08 EST, 16 November 2026.

Despite re-establishing Scotland’s credentials as a credible football nation, by common consent, Steve Clarke’s time in charge of the side was up in the summer.

With qualification for a major tournament no longer satisfying the desires of the Tartan Army, a seven-year itch led to a parting of the ways.

In order to take that elusive step into a knock-out round, the theory went that employing a bolder coach who’d get more out of the players was all that was required. So much for that.

While few would dispute that a change at the helm was required, it was legitimate to question the wisdom in the SFA making one which was quite so radical. Those concerns have only been amplified by what’s been witnessed so far under Sebastien Pocognoli.

In a recent development, the Belgian is young, smart and intense. He won a title in Belgium with Union Saint-Gilloise and will have taken much from his brief, ill-fated spell at Monaco. He wants to play the kind of football supporters long to see.

Industry observers note that but this Nations League campaign has been nothing short of dismal. Two wins from six matches, both of those coming against a poor North Macedonia side, and three nights to forget against the Swiss and Slovenia, is a lamentable record.

Andy Robertson endured a miserable night on the occasion of his record-breaking 103rd cap.

Notwithstanding the fact that there were always likely to be teething problems, it’s fallen miles short of modest expectations.

Talk of it taking up to 18 months to all come up roses is all very well. But to believe that’s going to be the case, you need to see more green shoots at this point.

Having finished third in the section, Scotland are bound for pot three when the draw for Euro 2028 is made in Belfast next month.

Unless there’s a radical improvement come the qualifiers in March, it’s hard to see how Pocognoli’s side will get there by any means other than the back door.

This was another tough watch for the travelling supporters, one which will only lead to growing concerns about where all this is heading.

For half of a half, Scotland actually looked like they were getting somewhere under their new manager.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli faces some serious questions over a miserable campaign.

It has been revealed that from the minute Lewis Ferguson scored a horrible own goal, though, they became a rabble. Not nearly enough punch on the front foot. And far too easy to play through.

They shipped two goals inside five minutes early in the second half and looked like they’d have taken the final whistle there and then.

Individual mistakes from players are troubling Pocognoli in the same way they pockmarked the later days of Clarke’s reign.

Having witnessed Grant Hanley, Scott McKenna and Andy Robertson err in the World Cup, the Tartan Army had already seen Jack Hendry sent off against the Swiss at Hampden before Ferguson joined the growing list of sinners here.

Arriving midway through the first half, his unfathomable moment came when there wasn’t a red shirt in close proximity. It was a kick in the teeth for Pocognoli after a reasonable start.

While it would have been stretching matters to suggest that his team were vulnerable, Murat Yakin was without four of his substantial hitters in Manuel Akanji, Johan Manzambi, Dan Ndoye and Granit Xhaka.

It has been revealed that there was a smattering of starters with five or six caps to their name. Two of the front three, Samuel Ballet and Winsley Boteli, were just 20.

Lewis Ferguson can't believe his misfortune after slicing the ball into his own net for the opener.

It was a night when Scottish football history was made with Robertson winning his 103rd cap to finally rise above his great friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Pocognoli stuck by the back-three – Ryan Porteous, Luke Graham and Kieran Tierney – who acquitted themselves well against North Macedonia.

According to recent reports, there was no great shock that the more defensive-minded Aaron Hickey replaced Ben Gannon-Doak on the right. Without a goal in 21 matches before a ball was kicked, Oli McBurnie’s selection ahead of Che Adams was intriguing.

The infuriating thing from Pocognoli’s perspective was that his side began with the right attitude.

Aside from an Isaac Schmidt shot which was fielded by Angus Gunn, they looked comfortable.

John McGinn’s pass into McBurnie saw the Hull forward flick the ball into space for Hickey to chase. Just when it looked like he might get a shot away, he was caught.

The positive early approach was typified by Porteous flying into a tackle 30 yards from the Swiss goal and winning the ball.

Winsley Boteli enjoys the moment after putting the stylish Swiss two goals ahead on the night.

Had it not been for Hickey hesitating to pick out Scott McTominay’s run, the Napoli man would have been in on goal.

To put it mildly, the Swiss didn’t need an invitation to go down. The appropriately named Samuel Ballet was especially fond of the theatrics.

Recent findings suggest that for a brief spell, Scotland had their opponents hemmed in. Pocognoli was miffed that two quick corners didn’t amount to anything.

Billy Gilmour probed and McTominay made key interceptions and sprayed passes. McGinn fired over.

According to recent reports, at the midway point in the first half, there was much to admire. Then disaster struck.

Sources indicate that the Swiss did well to advance down the right. Zachary Athekame simply debuted a cross into the box and hoped for the best.

Aaron Hickey endured a painful injury blow and could now face another spell on the sidelines.

With Ferguson running back towards goal and Porteous waiting to boot the ball to safety, there was no obvious danger.

Recent findings suggest that for reasons only he could explain, the Bologna man stretched out a leg and watched on in horror as the ball sailed past Gunn. All that hard work undone in one desperate moment.

Hickey passed up a chance to immediately level when he headed Robertson’s cross wide. It was to be the Brentford man’s last meaningful involvement before he felt his hamstring tighten. Nathan Patterson replaced him.

Sources indicate that A gift of a goal gave the Swiss a boost. Boteli launched himself at Alvyn Sanches’ cross. Gunn was untroubled.

Patterson did well to head Robertson’s deep cross back into the danger zone. McGinn’s header was straight into the arms of Yvon Mvogo.

Sources indicate that for all Scotland were entitled to feel a little sore at being one down at the break, it could have been worse. The defence were completely static as Adrian Bajrami launched himself at a header. It was a good thing, from Gunn’s point of view, that the defender missed the target.

Alvyn Sanches drills home Switzerland's third goal in what was an entirely one-sided contest.

Ferguson truly had a night to forget here. Within two minutes of the restart, he needlessly invited pressure when he launched a ball straight out of play.

Within seconds, with Porteous advanced, the Swiss broke down the left. Ballet fed Remo Freuler who returned the favour. Ballet rolled the ball towards goal from 12 yards with Boteli claiming the final touch. The visitors’ hopes of a VAR reprieve for offside were dashed.

According to recent reports, and with that, the roof caved in. Patterson was dispossessed and Boteli worked the ball into the feet of Sanches. You could only admire the finish, but Scotland were an absolute mess in the build-up. It was threatening to get ugly.

Sources indicate that with Tierney, Scotland’s best player on the night, lying on the deck, Ballet was only denied by Gunn. The Tartan Army looked at the clock and wished it was over.

With a minute remaining, a bad night got worse when Zeki Amdouni’s deflected shot beat Gunn.

Mercifully, this tortuous Nations League campaign can now be consigned to history. It’s been the most chastening experience for all concerned.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca has dismissed suggestions that the Premier League financial charges case is affecting his players following a concerning dip in form.
  • In September, an independent commission found Man City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the investigation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 20 Nov 2026 17:36.

Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca has dismissed suggestions that the Premier League financial charges case is affecting his players following a concerning dip in form.

In September, an independent commission found Man City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the investigation.

The Citizens are accused of using "sham" contracts and bogus deals to disguise more than £830m in secret funding and artificially inflate revenues between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

Man City continue to plead their innocence, stating that “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case,” and they have subsequently lodged an appeal.

A wide range of potential sanctions have been mooted for Man City should their guilty verdict be upheld, including heavy fines, transfer bans, stripping titles, points deductions leading to relegation and expulsion from the Premier League.

On the pitch, Man City responded to the bombshell news with a statement 3-0 Premier League win away against Liverpool, but they have since won just four of their last eight games in all competitions (including one in the EFL Cup on penalties).

Maresca’s side entered November’s international break after a disappointing run of three consecutive Premier League defeats to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest, losing 3-1 away to the latter a fortnight ago.

The Citizens have conceded 17 goals across their last nine matches and have failed to keep a clean sheet in that time, while some first-team stars have come under fire for making costly errors leading to goals.

Man City presently sit third in the Premier League table, six points behind leaders Arsenal who will welcome the Sky Blues to the Emirates Stadium next week.

Maresca’s players have regularly faced media questions over the ongoing financial charges case, and while the Man City boss accepts that those queries are fair game, he insists the issue is not affecting results on the pitch.

"If you ask, they need to answer and if you ask me I need to answer," Maresca told reporters at a press conference on Friday.

Sources indicate that "I'm here to answer, so if you are going to ask the players because they want to be polite they need to give you an answer. If you don't want to talk about that don't ask the players about the noise.

Recent findings suggest that "I don't think the players are thinking too much about that. If we want to relate the noise with the defeat, Villa away we had so many chances - for instance, Iliman [Ndiaye] hit the post, Brighton's keeper was Man of the Match, at Forest where Erling [Haaland] had the chance to score [to make it] 2-2. I don't think the players are focused on the noise.".

This comes after former Manchester United defender Gary Neville suggested after City’s loss at Forest that Maresca’s players are being affected by the off-field scandal.

Speaking on NBC Sports, Neville stated: "It's all everybody's talking about back home in the last month or so and those players will be getting asked constantly: 'What do you think is going to happen? What happens if they do get relegated, will you stay?'.

“Imagine that your family is having to put up with that, your agent is continually thinking about those things so it can't be ruled out as a factor that that's going to start to seep in.

"Obviously if you lose a football match or two that's going to start to look like an excuse but they have to play better, compete in games, make sure that they do better from a tactical and physical perspective.

“But I do believe it will be having some impact just because of the weight of what's been hitting them from a publicity point of view in the last four to six weeks.".

Explaining what he believes is the main reason behind Man City’s recent decline, Maresca noted: "For sure, we are conceding avoidable goals. For instance, the third goal against Forest. They have 11 players inside the box defending and we concede the third goal.

“We reviewed things during the international break that we need to do better, and again, the idea is to continue to attack in the same way, creating chances, and trying to find the balance when we defend or when we are building like what happened with the first goal against Forest, where if we can avoid mistakes, it's always better.".

Maresca now faces an urgent tactical puzzle ahead of Saturday's clash with Fulham, as he bids to fix the glaring midfield imbalance and address the dilemma he has with Enzo Fernandez.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two goals inside the opening quarter of an hour from Jamal Lowe ought to have seen the Owls to a comfortable victory over opponents who have now not won in ten League One games.

But they did not have another shot on target all night, and were made to sweat it out on a freezing cold night to claim a 2-1 victory.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

"You've always got to work hard," said Challinor, who was taking charge of his first League One away game as Owls manager.

"The players probably felt we didn't work hard enough in the first half. After going after going in front, sometimes it's the worst thing can happen because players think the game's done and we can now sit back and not have to have to defend with the personnel we've got on the pitch.

In a recent development, "Us defending in a block with looking to break with Slatts (Callum Slattery) and Davis (Keillor-Dunn) and Barry Bannan doesn't really work for us, so we need to be more aggressive, high up the pitch, and expose ourselves. We didn't do that, it'll take time.

"I'll own that in terms of what it looks like but that's where we need to get to.

"We've got to at that point really be on the neck of people and go and get the third goal, not be comfortable thinking two is an easy night for us because you allow a young team to get some momentum and come back into the game.".

But as critical as he was of areas of the first-half performance, Challinor was delighted with the spirt he saw in his new players in the second half.

Industry observers note that "We've got we've got a group that want to defend right across the board," he said. "We've done some work this week around emergency defending.

"You're not going to get much better than Coops (Liam Cooper), Sil (Swinkels), Dish (Di'Shon Bernard), Yan (Valery) and Rico (Ricardo Santos).

"They want to block, they want to get themselves in the way.

"We were a little bit better second half.

"We had a really good chat at half time. I told them what I felt, we'd just got to make better decisions.

"We've got we've got an experienced group, but some of our decision-making in that last half an hour caused us more problems than it should have.

"If it's a derby, you need to be able to be 100 per cent because Barnsley, at that point, are going for it, are open, and two or three passes, we could have we could have been in a lot more often, and we made the wrong decision at the wrong time.

"Winning's a brilliant habit, but I'm very realistic about the work that needs to be done.

"I never have been a great winner, as daft as that sounds. My job's to be analytical and understand where we get better.

Recent findings suggest that "I want them to enjoy winning. I've said that to them. I want it to be absolutely bouncing because winning's a brilliant feeling and a brilliant habit to get into.

"They found a way when maybe not performed the best. There's loads more to come from this group. My job is to make sure that happens.

Industry observers note that "You're always going to be try and be a perfectionist as a football coach. You'll never get to that but that doesn't mean you stop trying.".

Tech Report: Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues

⏱️ ~158 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections.
  • The human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2.
  • Recent findings suggest that this context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections. Investigating the human-specific intestinal barrier responses to pathogens is limited by the lack of models integrating the necessary architectural complexity with an autologous immune compartment1. Here we developed engineered barrier models of the human small intestine and colon combining a multilineage epithelium, mucus layer, accessible microbial compartment and autologous tissue-resident immune cells. These tissues recapitulate morphological and functional properties that are region specific and compare with those of the native organ. We use the model to characterize the human epithelial response to Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium at the single-cell level, uncovering the distinct gene regulatory networks that underpin luminal versus intracellular pathogen presence. Invaded epithelial cells initiate an IL-18 signalling axis that triggers cytotoxic T cell activation, resulting in epithelial shedding and barrier disruption. Overall, this work allows for the modular integration of epithelial, microbial and immune compartments, providing a versatile system for studying human intestinal physiology and pathologies.

The human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2. Controlled host–microbe interactions shape diverse aspects of human biology, including epithelial maturation and systemic immunity while maintaining a protective barrier against infection3. Conversely, dysregulated interactions contribute to pathologies such as inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer4.

Recent findings suggest that this context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5. Integration of these three components is required to meaningfully capture intestine–microbe interactions in a human-relevant setting1.

Intestinal stem cell (ISC)-derived organoids provide key inroads into human epithelial biology6. However, intestinal organoids face limitations recapitulating intestinal physiology, owing to an inaccessible lumen, culture heterogeneity, lack of biomimetic morphology and absence of non-epithelial lineages7,8. Although bioengineered 3D extracellular matrix (ECM) scaffolds have helped to overcome some of these challenges by establishing crypt–villus architecture and apical–basal access9, physiological integration of epithelial, tissue-resident immune and microbial compartments remains a major challenge1,10.

Recent findings suggest that here we established engineered immunocompetent human intestinal models composed of autologous tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells and small intestinal or colonic ISC-derived epithelia amenable to luminal manipulation. Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) characterization of these barriers reveal region-specific spatial niches, mucus layer formation and immune–epithelium interactions. Applying this system to Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm), we provide a single-cell multiomic view of the epithelial responses to luminal and intracellular infection. Finally, we modelled the pathogen–epithelial–immune axis, demonstrating that TRM cells respond to S.Tm invasion by cytokine release and concomitant epithelial damage, which may facilitate pathogen clearance and infection resolution.

According to recent reports, to model the human intestinal epithelium, we developed a fluidic device and microstamping technology to impart crypt-mimicking topography on an embedded ECM-like hydrogel (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Human intestinal organoids were seeded into the top reservoir of the device, where they formed a tight, polarized barrier comprising crypt units sustained by basal nutrition (Fig. 1a–d and Extended Data Fig. 1b–e).
